Earth's Interior, Rocks and Plate Tectonics
One theory explains quakes, mountains and oceans

Almost every physical-geography question in GS I leads back to plate tectonics . Earthquakes, volcanoes, fold mountains, ocean trenches and even the shape of India all follow from it. To answer well you need three things: what is inside the Earth, how we know, and how plates move. We take them in that order.
The layered Earth

We cannot drill beyond about 12 km. So scientists use indirect evidence: seismic waves , meteorites, gravity, magnetism and density. Crust is thin under oceans (about 5 km, basalt, called sima) and thick under continents (about 30 km, granite, called sial).
Discontinuities: where the layers change

A discontinuity is a boundary where seismic waves change speed or direction. The Moho was found in 1909 by the Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovicic. Know the pairs above: Moho, Gutenberg, Lehmann.
Seismic waves and the liquid core

P waves are primary, fast and longitudinal. S waves are secondary and transverse, and cannot pass through liquid. L waves travel on the surface and do the most damage. S waves vanish at the core. This proved the outer core is liquid.
Three rock families

Igneous rocks form from cooled magma. Intrusive ones such as granite cool slowly; extrusive ones such as basalt cool fast. Sedimentary rocks form from compacted sediments, often with fossils and layers, e.g. sandstone and limestone. Metamorphic rocks are changed by heat or pressure, e.g. marble from limestone and slate from shale.
Wegener and continental drift, 1912

Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912, and published in 1915, that all land once formed one supercontinent, Pangaea , in the ocean Panthalassa. It broke up about 200 million years ago. His evidence: the jigsaw fit of Africa and South America, matching rocks and fossils (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris), and glacial deposits across southern continents. His weakness: he could not explain the force that moved continents. Geologists rejected him.
Sea-floor spreading

In the early 1960s Harry Hess argued that new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads outward. Old crust sinks at trenches. Vine and Matthews (1963) found symmetrical magnetic stripes on either side of a ridge, recording reversals of Earth's field. Ocean floor is young: nowhere older than about 180 million years. Continents hold rocks over 4 billion years old.
Plate tectonics, late 1960s

The theory was assembled by McKenzie, Parker and Morgan (1967-68). The lithosphere (crust plus top mantle) is broken into 7 major plates (Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic) and many minor ones. Plates float on the soft asthenosphere .
What drives the plates?

Three ideas compete and probably work together: mantle convection (hot rock rising, cold sinking), slab pull (a heavy sinking plate drags the rest, thought to be strongest) and ridge push . Hotspots are fixed plumes in the mantle. Plates drift over them and leave volcanic chains, e.g. Hawaii. Critics note that the plume idea is still debated, and that the exact driving force is not fully settled.
India as a travelling plate

The Indian plate split from Gondwana and moved north at up to 15-20 cm a year before colliding with Eurasia about 50 million years ago. It still pushes at about 5 cm a year. This built the Himalaya , which is why they still rise and shake. Passing over the Reunion hotspot , India erupted the Deccan Traps about 66 million years ago. Subduction under Myanmar causes the Andaman volcanoes, including Barren Island, India's only active volcano.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the theory of plate tectonics and its role in explaining earthquakes and volcanoes." (15 marks) "How did the Himalaya form?" (10 marks) Structure: start with Wegener and Hess as the roots; give the plate idea; draw the three boundaries; link each to landforms; end with India's collision zone. Prelims tip: know which waves cannot pass through liquid (S), the depth of the Gutenberg discontinuity, and that the Indo-Australian plate is a single major plate in the usual list.
Earthquakes, Volcanoes and Tsunamis
The Earth moves, and people die

Quakes, volcanoes and tsunamis appear both in Physical Geography and in disaster management. India has had Latur (1993), Bhuj (2001), the 2004 tsunami and Nepal (2015). UPSC asks about causes, distribution and India's exposure.
How an earthquake works

Stress builds on a fault. Rock slips, and energy spreads as waves. Magnitude (Richter, now usually the moment scale) is logarithmic: each step is about 10 times the wave amplitude and about 32 times the energy. Intensity (Mercalli, I to XII) measures effects felt.
Where quakes strike
Quakes mostly follow plate boundaries. Shallow quakes happen at all boundaries. Deep ones only occur in subduction zones. Intraplate quakes (Latur, Bhuj) are rarer, along old buried faults.
Causes beyond plates

Volcanic quakes, collapse quakes (mines, caves) and reservoir-induced quakes also occur. The Koyna quake of 1967 (about M6.3) is the classic Indian case of reservoir-induced seismicity. Effects: ground shaking, liquefaction, landslides, fires, tsunamis. The shaking and poor building, not the quake itself, kills most people.
Volcanoes and their forms

A volcano is a vent where magma reaches the surface. Shield volcanoes (Mauna Loa) are broad with runny basalt. Composite cones (Fuji, Vesuvius) alternate lava and ash and are explosive. Caldera (Krakatoa, Toba) forms when a cone collapses. Flood basalts built the Deccan Traps.
Intrusive and extrusive forms

Magma cooling underground makes batholiths (big domes), laccoliths (lens with a flat base), sills (horizontal sheets) and dykes (vertical walls). Dykes are common in the Deccan. Surface forms include cones, lava plateaus and geysers and hot springs from heated ground water. Volcano status: active, dormant or extinct.
Tsunami

A tsunami (Japanese for harbour wave) is a series of waves from a sudden seabed shift, usually from a subduction quake, landslide or eruption. It is hardly seen in deep water. On reaching shallows it slows and rises. Hunga Tonga (2022) showed that eruptions can cause them too.
India's seismic map and the 2004 tsunami

The long-used BIS map (IS 1893, 2002) has four zones, II to V, with Zone V the highest. About 59% of India's land is quake-prone. A revised BIS code released in November 2025 adds a new Zone VI for the Himalayan arc, so check which map a question refers to. On 26 December 2004 a magnitude 9.1-9.3 quake off Sumatra sent waves to Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Kerala and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. India then set up the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre at INCOIS, Hyderabad (2007).
Can we predict earthquakes?

No. Science can give probabilities and hazard maps, not exact times. Early-warning systems exploit the gap between fast P waves and damaging S waves, giving seconds of notice. Real risk reduction comes from building codes , retrofitting, land-use rules and drills. After Bhuj (26 January 2001, M7.7) and Nepal (25 April 2015, M7.8) the debate shifted from nature to unsafe construction.
How to write this

Likely questions "Describe the distribution of volcanoes and earthquakes in the world." (10 marks) "Why is the Himalayan region prone to earthquakes? How do they differ from the Peninsular ones?" (15 marks) Structure: define; give causes; map the Pacific and Alpine belts; add Indian zones; end with mitigation (codes, early warning, drills). Prelims tip: Richter is logarithmic; Mercalli measures intensity; Barren Island is India's only active volcano; Koyna is the reservoir-induced example.
Landforms and Geomorphic Processes
Landforms are the Earth's fingerprints

Every hill, delta and dune is the result of a tug of war between forces that build land and forces that wear it down. GS I asks for this reasoning, often through Indian examples such as ravines, karst or the Sundarbans.
Endogenic and exogenic forces

Endogenic forces (volcanism, folding, faulting) create relief. Exogenic forces (weathering, erosion, transport, deposition) reduce it. Landforms are the net result. Sudden endogenic events are earthquakes and volcanoes; slow ones are mountain building and warping.
Weathering and mass movement

Weathering breaks rock in place, with no transport. Physical (frost, exfoliation from day-night heating), chemical (oxidation, carbonation, solution) and biological types act together. Warm, wet climates favour chemical action, giving thick soils and laterite . Mass movement is the downslope shift of material under gravity: creep, flow, slide, fall. Heavy rain, steep slopes and cut roads trigger Himalayan landslides.
Running water: the strongest agent

Rivers cut valleys upstream and deposit downstream. Key forms: waterfalls (Jog on the Sharavati, Hogenakkal), meanders, oxbow lakes, alluvial fans where a river leaves hills, and deltas where it meets the sea. Rivers hit by a base-level fall or uplift cut deep gorges.
Glaciers

Ice cuts U-shaped valleys , scoops cirques , and leaves sharp arete ridges and pyramid horns (Matterhorn). It dumps moraines , and shapes drumlins and eskers . Siachen, Gangotri and Zemu are Indian glaciers. Kumaon-Garhwal glacial lakes and "hanging valleys" are common.
Wind, groundwater and sea

Wind works in dry lands: deflation hollows, mushroom rocks, yardangs, crescent barchans and fine loess deposits (China). Groundwater in limestone makes karst : sinkholes, caves, stalactites. Waves build cliffs, stacks, spits and bars, and form beaches.
Major relief types

Mountains: fold (Himalaya, Alps), block or horst (Vosges, Black Forest), volcanic (Fuji), and residual or relict (Aravalli, Nilgiri). Plateaus: intermontane (Tibet), piedmont and continental (Deccan). Plains: erosional (peneplain) and depositional (Indo-Gangetic, alluvial). The Aravalli are among the oldest fold ranges, now worn down. The Rift valley of the Narmada and Tapi is a down-faulted block, a graben.
Davis, Penck and the cycle of erosion

W.M. Davis (1899) proposed a "cycle": uplift, then youth, maturity and old age ending in a flat peneplain. Walther Penck (1924) argued uplift and erosion work together, so slopes retreat in parallel. Critics say Davis assumed a quick uplift followed by a calm period. Modern geomorphology favours dynamic equilibrium and human activity as a driver: mining, dams and farming now move more earth than many rivers.
Indian landforms at a glance

Ravines and badlands: Chambal and Yamuna, formed by gully erosion in soft alluvium. Barchans: Thar. Karst: Meghalaya (Mawsmai and Krem Liat Prah caves), Chhattisgarh (Kutumsar) and Borra caves in Andhra Pradesh. Delta: Ganga-Brahmaputra, the world's largest, with the Sundarbans mangroves. Coastal erosion eats Kerala's shores. Himalayan landslides, as at Joshimath (2023, subsidence), show human pressure on fragile slopes.
How to write this

Likely questions "Explain the role of running water in shaping the Indian landscape." (10 marks) "Differentiate between weathering, erosion and mass wasting." (10 marks) Structure: split into endogenic and exogenic; then agent by agent, with a landform and an Indian example each. Prelims tip: know the agent behind each landform (U-valley = glacier, barchan = wind, stalactite = groundwater, oxbow = river).
Fluvial, Glacial and Aeolian Landforms
Same rock, different sculptor

Landforms are made by agents of gradation : running water, ice, wind, waves and groundwater. UPSC asks you to name a landform, say which agent made it and where it is found. If you link each landform to its agent and stage, you can answer almost any question in this area.
Three agents, three signatures

Each agent works in two steps: erosion (wearing away) and deposition (laying down). Rivers cut V-shaped valleys. Glaciers cut U-shaped valleys. Wind cuts hollows and builds dunes. The shape of the valley is the quickest clue to the agent. Remember: agents work best in specific climates. Rivers dominate humid regions, ice dominates cold and high regions, wind dominates dry regions.
River stages: youth, maturity, old age

W M Davis proposed the cycle of erosion in 1899. In youth the river cuts down: waterfalls, rapids, gorges and V-shaped valleys. In maturity it widens its valley and forms meanders. In old age it deposits: floodplains, levees, oxbow lakes, deltas. Critics say the cycle is too tidy. Real rivers can show all stages at once and tectonic uplift can restart the cycle. This is called rejuvenation .
Fluvial erosional landforms

Waterfalls form where a hard rock layer overlies soft rock. Potholes are drilled by swirling pebbles. Gorges and canyons form in dry, uplifted rock (Grand Canyon on the Colorado). River terraces are old floodplains left high after uplift. Incised meanders show a rejuvenated river. In India, Jog (Gersoppa) Falls on the Sharavati and Chitrakoot Falls on the Indravati are classic waterfalls. The Brahmaputra cuts a deep gorge round the Namcha Barwa.
Fluvial depositional landforms

Alluvial fans form where a river leaves a mountain. Levees are natural banks built in floods. Oxbow lakes are cut-off meander loops (Kanwar Lake in Bihar is one). Deltas form when a river drops its load at the sea. The three delta shapes are arcuate (Nile), bird's foot (Mississippi) and estuarine. The Ganga-Brahmaputra delta in the Sundarbans is the largest in the world. It is tide-dominated and mostly covered in mangrove.
Glacial landforms: erosion

Glaciers pluck and grind rock. They make cirques (armchair hollows), arêtes (knife-edge ridges), horns (pyramid peaks like the Matterhorn), U-shaped valleys and hanging valleys that end in waterfalls. A drowned glacial valley is a fjord , seen in Norway, Chile and New Zealand. In the Himalaya, glacial valleys are found around Gangotri and Siachen. Siachen, about 70 km long, is one of the longest glaciers outside the polar regions.
Glacial landforms: deposition

Rock debris carried by ice is called till , and its ridges are moraines : lateral, medial, terminal. Streamlined hills of till are drumlins . Winding sand ridges laid by meltwater streams are eskers . Large lone boulders left behind are erratics . Meltwater also leaves kettle lakes . The Great Lakes of North America and the lakes of Finland are glacial in origin. Kashmir's Karewas are lake deposits from the Pleistocene, famous for saffron.
Aeolian (wind) landforms

Wind erodes by deflation (lifting loose sand) and abrasion (sand-blasting). It makes deflation hollows , mushroom rocks , yardangs and inselbergs . Deposits include barchan (crescent dunes), seif (longitudinal dunes) and loess (fine wind-blown silt). Loess covers northern China and is highly fertile. Barchan dunes in the Thar move with the southwest monsoon wind. Dunes advance a few metres a year and threaten fields.
Where to find them in India

Thar : barchans, playas (salt lakes like Sambhar and Didwana), and the Luni as the one major river. Karst-like cave landscapes : Meghalaya, with Mawsmai caves, and Borra caves in Andhra Pradesh. Glacial : Gangotri, Pindari, Siachen. Fluvial deltas : Ganga, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery. Ravines : the Chambal badlands in Madhya Pradesh, where gully erosion cuts deep.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Differentiate glacial and fluvial landforms', 'Explain the formation of a delta', 'Wind erosion landforms in hot deserts'. Start with the agent, then process, then landform, then a named place. Use a quick sketch of a V valley beside a U valley. Link to human use: deltas for rice, loess for wheat, moraines for lakes.
Folds, Faults and Mountain Building
Mountains are a repeated UPSC theme

Questions ask how fold mountains form, why the Himalaya are still rising, and how block mountains differ. These are classic 'explain with a diagram' answers. The idea underneath is simple: rocks bend or break when squeezed or pulled .
Stress makes folds and faults

Compression pushes rock together and makes folds. Tension pulls rock apart and makes faults. Plastic rock bends. Brittle rock breaks. The same force can do either, depending on rock type, depth and speed. An anticline is an upfold (arch). A syncline is a downfold (trough). An overfold is a fold pushed over to one side. A nappe is a huge recumbent fold, found in the Alps and Himalaya.
Types of mountains

Four classes: fold (Himalaya, Alps, Rockies, Andes), block (Vosges, Black Forest, Sierra Nevada), volcanic (Mt Fuji, Mt Kilimanjaro) and residual or relict (Aravalli, Nilgiri, Vindhya). Fold mountains are the youngest and highest. Residual mountains are old, worn-down remains of earlier uplifts or plateaus cut by rivers.
Faults and what they build

A fault is a break along which rock moves. Normal faults pull the crust apart. Reverse (thrust) faults push it together. Strike-slip faults slide sideways (San Andreas). A raised block between faults is a horst . A sunken block is a graben . A graben that fills with water forms a rift valley : the Rhine, the Great Rift Valley of East Africa, the Dead Sea.
Geosyncline theory

James Hall (1859) and James Dana studied the Appalachians. They said sediment piles up in long shallow troughs called geosynclines . Later, squeezing folds and uplifts that sediment into mountains. Kober (1921) called the rigid blocks around the trough forelands and the squeezing movement an orogen . Plate tectonics replaced this idea in the 1960s, but the language of geosynclines survives in textbooks.
Plate tectonics explains mountain building

Fold mountains form at convergent boundaries . In continent-continent collision (India and Eurasia) neither plate sinks easily, so the crust crumples and thickens: the Himalaya. In ocean-continent convergence the denser oceanic plate subducts: the Andes and Rockies, with volcanoes. Where plates are pulled apart, block mountains and rift valleys form.
How the Himalaya formed

The Indian plate broke from Gondwana about 120 million years ago and moved north. Its collision with Eurasia started about 50 million years ago. The Tethys sea sediments were squeezed into the Himalaya in three phases: Himadri, Himachal, Shiwalik (Miocene to Pliocene). India still moves north at around 5 cm a year. That is why the Himalaya are rising and earthquake-prone.
Are the Himalaya still rising?

Yes. GPS data show uplift of roughly a few millimetres a year in parts. But erosion by glaciers and rivers removes a lot of rock. The net height of Everest changes little. China and Nepal re-measured Everest in 2020 and announced 8,848.86 m. Remember: rising does not mean growing taller without limit. Uplift and erosion fight each other.
India's mountain types

Fold : Himalaya, Purvanchal. Residual : Aravalli (among the oldest fold mountains, now worn), Vindhya, Satpura, Nilgiri. Block : Satpura is a horst between the Narmada and Tapi rift valleys. These two rivers flow in rift valleys (grabens) and so form estuaries, not deltas. The Western Ghats are the edge of a fault-scarp, formed by faulting along the west coast.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Explain the origin of the Himalaya', 'Distinguish between fold and block mountains', 'Why do the Narmada and Tapi form estuaries?' Draw plates colliding with arrows and label compression. Give three examples for each type of mountain. Close with a hazard link: earthquakes along the Main Central Thrust.
Atmosphere, Insolation and Heat Budget
Climate begins with the sun
Monsoon, deserts, cyclones and global warming all start with one question: how much solar energy reaches a place, and where does it go? The heat budget is the answer and a UPSC favourite.
What air is made of

Dry air by volume: nitrogen 78% , oxygen 21% , argon 0.93%, carbon dioxide about 0.04% (over 420 ppm as of the mid-2020s, rising). Water vapour varies from 0 to 4%. Dust, salt and pollen act as hygroscopic nuclei for cloud formation. Gases are held by gravity. About 99% of air lies within 32 km of the ground.
Layers of the atmosphere

Boundaries are called pauses : tropopause, stratopause and so on. The tropopause is higher at the equator (about 18 km) than at the poles (about 8 km). Weather happens only in the troposphere. The ozone layer sits at 15 to 35 km.
Insolation: what controls it

Insolation is incoming solar radiation, mostly short-wave. It depends on: the angle of rays (equator gets near-vertical rays), length of day , the transparency of air (clouds, dust), and the Sun-Earth distance. Earth is nearest the Sun ( perihelion ) in early January and farthest ( aphelion ) in early July. Season, not distance, makes summer and winter, because Earth's axis is tilted by 23.5 degrees.
The heat budget
Earth neither heats up nor cools down overall, so incoming and outgoing energy balance. Greenhouse gases keep the average surface near 15 C instead of about -18 C.
How heat moves

Conduction : contact, mostly at the ground. Convection : vertical air currents. Advection : horizontal movement, which is more important in weather, e.g. the hot dry Loo of north India. Latent heat : heat released when vapour condenses, which fuels cyclones.
Lapse rate and inversion
Inversions form on long, clear, calm winter nights with snow cover. They trap smoke in valleys. Mountain-side inversions favour orchards mid-slope because cold air drains downhill.
Greenhouse effect: natural versus enhanced

The natural effect is useful. Human burning of fossil fuels adds CO2 and methane, thickening the blanket. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to hold warming well below 2 C and pursue 1.5 C. Critics note that India, with low per capita emissions, argues for common but differentiated responsibilities . Ozone depletion is a separate problem: the Montreal Protocol (1987) phases out CFCs; the Kigali Amendment (2016) phases down HFCs.
Indian examples

The Tropic of Cancer passes through eight states (Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram). The Loo, pre-monsoon heat waves (IMD flags them above 40 C in plains) and Delhi winter smog from inversions and stubble burning all follow from this lesson. The Indo-Gangetic Plain is one of the world's most polluted air basins.
How to write this

Likely questions "Explain the heat budget of the Earth." (10 marks) "What is temperature inversion? Discuss its effects." (10 marks) Structure: define; draw the 100-unit diagram; explain the balance; link to greenhouse warming; give an Indian example. Prelims tip: ozone is in the stratosphere; the ionosphere reflects radio waves; the tropopause is highest at the equator; albedo is 35%.
Pressure Belts, Winds and Jet Streams
Why the wind blows where it does
Pressure differences drive winds. Winds move heat, moisture and cyclones, and shape rainfall from the Sahara to the Ganga. The Indian monsoon is simply a seasonal swing of this global system.
Pressure belts

Pressure rises where air sinks and falls where air rises. Thermal causes explain the equatorial low and polar highs. Dynamic causes (Earth's spin, sinking air) explain the subtropical highs and subpolar lows. Belts shift north and south with the Sun, about 5 to 10 degrees.
Coriolis force and wind direction

Earth's rotation deflects moving air to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern ( Ferrel's law ). The force is zero at the equator and greatest at the poles. Winds are named by where they come from. A westerly comes from the west. Winds blow from high to low pressure, and the closer the isobars, the stronger the wind.
Planetary winds

Trade winds blow towards the equator and carry steady weather. Westerlies are strong and stormy in the southern oceans: Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, Screaming Sixties. Polar easterlies are cold and dry.
Three-cell model
At the ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone) trades from both hemispheres meet and rise, forming huge cloud and rain bands. Its seasonal shift north over India is central to the monsoon.
Jet streams
Jets sit just below the tropopause, where air temperature contrasts are sharp.
Local winds

Land and sea breeze : day sea breeze, night land breeze. Valley and mountain winds . Katabatic : cold air draining downslope. Foehn (Alps) and Chinook (Rockies): warm, dry downslope winds that melt snow. Mistral : cold, from the Alps to the Mediterranean. Harmattan : dry dust wind from the Sahara.
Is the jet stream weakening?

Some studies link a warming Arctic to a wavier polar jet, with longer cold spells and heat domes. Others find the evidence mixed. The safe exam position: it is a research debate, but jets clearly shape extremes such as western disturbances and heat waves.
Jets and Indian weather

In winter the subtropical westerly jet shifts south of the Himalaya and steers western disturbances , giving rain and snow in the north-west (good for rabi wheat). In summer it moves north of the Tibetan plateau and the tropical easterly jet helps the burst of the monsoon. Local winds: Loo in north India, Kalbaisakhi (Nor'wester) in Bengal, Mango showers in Kerala and Karnataka.
How to write this

Likely questions "What are jet streams and how do they affect the weather and climate of India?" (10 marks) "Explain the general circulation of the atmosphere." (15 marks) Structure: pressure belts with cause; the three cells; winds; jets; then India (western disturbances, monsoon burst). Prelims tip: the tropical easterly jet is a summer feature; Ferrel's law gives right deflection in the northern hemisphere; Chinook is in North America.
Clouds, Precipitation and Cyclones
Cyclones kill and clouds feed

Rain feeds farms; cyclones destroy them. The same physics of rising moist air gives both. UPSC asks about types of rainfall, cyclone formation and India's cyclone record, often as short 10-mark questions.
Humidity, dew point and condensation

Absolute humidity is vapour weight per volume. Relative humidity is the percentage of what the air could hold at that temperature. When air cools to its dew point it is saturated and condenses on nuclei. Clouds are tiny water drops or ice crystals. Warm air holds more vapour. Cooling happens by rising, by contact with cold surfaces, or by mixing.
Clouds
Remember: cirro = high, alto = middle, strato = layered, cumulo = heaped, nimbo = rain-bearing.
Three kinds of rainfall

Convectional : heated ground, rising moist air, afternoon showers in the tropics. Orographic : air forced up a mountain. Cyclonic or frontal : air lifted along a front or a low-pressure centre. Hail forms in strong updraughts in cumulonimbus.
How a tropical cyclone forms

Conditions: sea surface above about 26.5 C , high humidity, a small-scale disturbance, low vertical wind shear and a Coriolis force strong enough (more than about 5 degrees from the equator). Heat from condensing vapour feeds the storm.
Naming and classification

Names are given by regional bodies. For the north Indian Ocean the RSMC at IMD, New Delhi assigns names from lists supplied by member countries (since 2004). Storm surge, not wind, causes most deaths.
Tropical and temperate cyclones
Temperate cyclones form where warm and cold air meet along a front . The cold front overtakes the warm front and the system occludes . Western disturbances are the Indian version.
India's cyclone record

Eastern coast (Bay of Bengal) gets more and stronger cyclones, mostly in October to November and April to May. Landfalls: Odisha super cyclone (1999), Phailin (2013), Fani (2019), Amphan (2020). The Arabian Sea has become more active: Tauktae (2021), Biparjoy (2023). Odisha's early warning and mass evacuation cut deaths from tens of thousands in 1999 to under 50 in Phailin, a model for the world.
Is climate change making cyclones worse?

Warmer seas add fuel. Studies suggest more intense storms and rapid intensification , especially in the Arabian Sea, though total numbers may not rise. Rising sea levels worsen surge flooding. The sound answer: intensity and rainfall likely increase; frequency is uncertain.
How to write this

Likely questions "Why are tropical cyclones more frequent in the Bay of Bengal than in the Arabian Sea?" (10 marks) "Differentiate between tropical and temperate cyclones." (10 marks) Structure: conditions; mechanism; classification; Indian cases; then mitigation (early warning, shelters, mangroves). Prelims tip: a cyclone does not form on the equator; RSMC New Delhi names north Indian Ocean storms; the eye is calm.
Climate Types and El Niño
Climate is not just weather

Weather is what happens today. Climate is the average over about 30 years. Classifying climates gives a language for vegetation, farming and settlement. El Nino explains why some monsoons fail. Both are everyday GS I questions.
Koppen's scheme

Wladimir Koppen (first version 1884, revised 1918 and 1936) used temperature, rainfall and natural vegetation. Small letters add detail: f wet all year, w dry winter, s dry summer, h hot, k cold. Highland climates are labelled H.
Tropical climates: A

Af equatorial: rain every day, dense forest (Amazon, Congo). Am monsoon: short dry spell (Kerala, Bangladesh). Aw savanna: dry winter, grass and scattered trees (Sudan, Brazilian campos, most of peninsular India). Annual temperature range is small near the equator; diurnal range is bigger than annual range.
Dry and temperate climates: B and C

BWh hot desert (Sahara, Thar) at about 30 degrees on west coasts where cold currents add dryness. BS steppe is the grassy fringe. Cs Mediterranean: wet winters, dry summers (California, Chile, Cape). Cfa China type: humid subtropical. Cfb British type: mild, rain all year, on west coasts at 40-60 degrees.
Cold and polar: D and E

Df cold with year-round precipitation: Siberia and Canada, the coniferous taiga . Winter is very long and the annual range of temperature is the largest on Earth. ET tundra and EF ice cap. Permafrost thaw is now a climate worry.
El Nino and the Walker circulation

El Nino is unusual warming of the central and eastern Pacific, first noticed off Peru near Christmas (el nino means the boy child). The paired atmospheric change is the Southern Oscillation, so together they are ENSO .
ENSO and the Indian Ocean Dipole

La Nina brings the reverse. India's monsoon is often weak in El Nino years (2002, 2009, 2014, 2015) but not always: 1997 was normal. A positive IOD can offset El Nino, as in 2019 with a strong positive IOD.
Is climate prediction a gamble?

ENSO is now forecast months ahead, helping farmers and the government stock grain. But the link to India is not one-to-one, because the IOD, the Madden-Julian Oscillation and Eurasian snow also matter. Some studies suggest climate change makes ENSO extremes stronger. Treat claims with care.
India's climates and El Nino

Koppen's map for India: Am (Malabar), Aw (peninsula), BShw (semi-arid Deccan rain shadow), BWhw (Thar), Cwg (Gangetic plain), Dfc (Arunachal), and E (high Himalaya). Years like 2015 and 2023 (El Nino) brought below-normal rain; 2023 monsoon was about 94% of the long-period average. IMD now uses Mission Mausam (approved 2024) to improve forecasts.
How to write this

Likely questions "Describe the characteristics and distribution of the Mediterranean climate." (10 marks) "What is El Nino? How does it affect the Indian monsoon?" (10 marks) Structure: define; explain the normal Walker cell; show the break; list global effects; then India (monsoon, crops, prices, policy response). Prelims tip: Mediterranean = west coasts at 30-45 degrees; Peru's coast is where El Nino was first noticed; positive IOD aids the monsoon.
Koppen's Climate Classification
One code describes a whole climate

Wladimir Koppen, a German-Russian climatologist, published his scheme from 1900 and refined it until 1936. Rudolf Geiger later modified it, so it is often written Koppen-Geiger. UPSC uses it to ask where a climate occurs and why, and to test map knowledge across continents.
How the code works

Koppen used temperature and rainfall only, because natural vegetation reflects them. Each climate gets a letter code. The first letter gives the main group. The second gives the rain pattern. The third gives the temperature detail. Example: Am means tropical monsoon. Cwa means humid subtropical with dry winter and hot summer.
Five main groups

A Tropical: coldest month above 18 degrees C. B Dry: evaporation exceeds rain. C Warm temperate: coldest month between 18 and minus 3. D Cold snow-forest: coldest below minus 3, warmest above 10. E Polar: warmest month below 10. A sixth group, H , covers highland climates.
Group A: tropical

Af : tropical wet, rain all year (Amazon, Congo, Indonesia). Am : monsoon, short dry season (Kerala, Konkan, Bangladesh). Aw : tropical wet and dry, or savanna, with a dry winter (central India, Brazilian plateau, East Africa). The letters f, m, w stand for 'feucht' (wet), 'monsoon' and 'winter dry'.
Group B: dry

BW is arid desert and BS is semi-arid steppe. A third letter shows temperature: h hot, k cold. So BWh is a hot desert (Sahara, Thar) and BSk is a cold steppe (Great Plains, Kazakh steppe). Koppen used a formula comparing annual rain to temperature to separate dry from humid climates.
Group C and D

C: Cs Mediterranean (dry summer: California, Chile, Cape Town, Mediterranean coast), Cw warm with dry winter (north India plains), Cf humid temperate (western Europe, southeast USA). D: Df cold with no dry season (Russia, Canada), Dw cold with dry winter (Siberia, Mongolia, northeast China). Group D exists only in the northern hemisphere, because the southern hemisphere has little land at those latitudes.
Group E: polar
ET is tundra: warmest month between 0 and 10 degrees C. Mosses, lichens, no trees. EF is ice cap: all months below 0 degrees C. Antarctica and interior Greenland.
Strengths and limits

Strengths : simple, uses data anyone can measure, matches vegetation closely. Limits : ignores wind, cloud and causes of climate. It is empirical, not genetic. Thornthwaite (1931, revised 1948) used the water balance. Trewartha later cut group C and D boundaries to better fit continental interiors.
Koppen's India

India has six types. Amw : monsoon with short dry season (Malabar and Konkan coast). As : dry summer, rain in winter (Coromandel coast). Aw : tropical savanna (most of the peninsula). BShw : semi-arid steppe (rain shadow of Western Ghats, Gujarat, Rajasthan east). BWhw : hot desert (west Rajasthan). Cwg : warm humid with dry winter (Ganga plain). Dfc and E : Himalaya.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Compare tropical monsoon and savanna climates', 'Why is Mediterranean climate found on west coasts at 30-40 degrees?', 'Koppen's classification of India'. Always give the code, the criterion and two regions. Explain the location with pressure belts shifting seasonally. Mention its limits to show critical thinking.
Air Masses, Fronts and Temperate Cyclones
Weather in mid-latitudes is a story of collisions

A huge body of air takes on the heat and moisture of the surface beneath it. When two such bodies meet, they make a front and a storm. This lesson links to western disturbances in India, to Europe's weather and to winter rain in the Mediterranean. It is a steady source of conceptual questions.
What is an air mass?

An air mass is a large body of air, often 1,600 km or more across, with nearly uniform temperature and humidity at any height. It forms over a source region that is flat, uniform and under light winds: the polar ice, the Sahara, the warm oceans. Names use two letters. First: c continental (dry) or m maritime (moist). Second: T tropical, P polar, A arctic, E equatorial.
Five major air masses

mT maritime tropical: warm, moist, over warm oceans. cT continental tropical: hot, dry, over deserts. mP maritime polar: cool and moist. cP continental polar: cold and dry. cA continental arctic: very cold, from the ice sheets. Indian monsoon is driven by mE (maritime equatorial) air flowing in from the southern Indian Ocean.
Fronts

A front is the sloping boundary between two unlike air masses. The warmer, lighter air rises over the colder, denser air. This lifting makes cloud and rain. Cold front : cold air pushes under warm. Steep slope, short heavy rain, thunder. Warm front : warm air slides over cold. Gentle slope, long steady drizzle. Stationary front : neither moves. Occluded front : a cold front catches a warm front.
Frontogenesis and the polar front

The creation of a front is frontogenesis . Its decay is frontolysis . The main global front is the polar front , where cold polar easterlies meet warm westerlies near 60 degrees N and S. The Norwegian meteorologist Vilhelm Bjerknes and colleagues developed the polar front theory around 1918-1920. 'Front' was chosen by analogy with the battle fronts of World War I.
Life of a temperate cyclone

A temperate (extratropical) cyclone grows along the polar front through stages: initial, incipient, mature, occlusion and dissipation. A wave forms on the front. Warm air flows into a pocket, called the warm sector , between a cold and a warm front. Pressure falls at the centre. The cold front moves faster and eventually overtakes the warm front. The cyclone then dies.
Tropical vs temperate cyclones

Tropical cyclones are smaller (100-500 km), form only over warm seas above about 26.5 degrees C, have an eye, and weaken over land. Temperate cyclones are much larger (up to 2,000 km), can form over land or sea, have no eye, move west to east with the westerlies, and have fronts. Tropical ones have a warm core. Temperate ones have a cold core in the upper air and are driven by temperature contrast.
Anticyclones and blocking

An anticyclone is a high-pressure system: clear skies, light winds, dry weather. Winds blow clockwise in the north and anticlockwise in the south. It brings summer heat and winter cold waves. When an anticyclone stalls for days, it blocks the usual westerly flow and causes heatwaves or floods nearby, such as the European heatwave of 2003.
What it means for India

The western disturbance is an extratropical storm born over the Mediterranean and carried east by the subtropical westerly jet. It brings winter rain to northwest India and snow to the Himalaya. Cold fronts also help produce cold waves in Punjab and Haryana. Air mass thinking explains the monsoon too: the arrival of mE air.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Differentiate tropical and temperate cyclones', 'Explain the formation of fronts', 'Role of air masses in weather'. Use a table with five rows: origin, size, eye, movement, season. Draw a warm sector with the two fronts. Link to western disturbances for the Indian marks.
Indian Ocean Dipole, La Nina and Teleconnections
India's monsoon is tied to distant oceans

The Indian monsoon is not driven only by local heating. Sea temperatures in the Pacific and Indian Oceans shape it year to year. UPSC has asked about El Nino, La Nina and the Indian Ocean Dipole more than once. Learn the three systems together as teleconnections : climate links between far-apart places.
ENSO in one paragraph

ENSO (El Nino Southern Oscillation) is a Pacific cycle. Normally trade winds push warm water west, piling it up near Indonesia, while cold water upwells off Peru. In El Nino the trades weaken, warm water slides east, and the Walker circulation shifts. In La Nina the trades strengthen and the normal pattern grows stronger. The 'Southern Oscillation' is the pressure see-saw between Tahiti and Darwin, found by Gilbert Walker in the 1920s.
Walker circulation

The Walker cell is an east-west loop over the equatorial Pacific. Air rises over the warm western Pacific and sinks over the cool east. During El Nino it weakens or reverses. Rain moves east, so Indonesia, Australia and India tend to get less. Sinking air over the Indian Ocean side suppresses monsoon rain in many El Nino years.
La Nina

La Nina means 'the girl'. Pacific water off Peru turns unusually cold. India often gets a good monsoon and a colder winter in the north. Australia sees floods. The southwest US gets drought. Years can be neutral . Neither pattern always matches the monsoon: India had normal rain in some El Nino years.
Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)

The IOD is a see-saw in sea surface temperature between the western Indian Ocean (off Africa) and the eastern part (off Sumatra). Saji and colleagues named it in 1999. Positive IOD : western Indian Ocean warmer, east cooler. Good for the Indian monsoon, heavy rain in East Africa, drought in Indonesia and Australia. Negative IOD : the opposite. Weaker Indian monsoon.
IOD can cancel El Nino

In 1997 a strong El Nino was expected to hurt India, yet the monsoon was normal. A strong positive IOD compensated. In 2019 a record positive IOD helped a late but very heavy monsoon despite a weak El Nino. Remember: the IOD can offset El Nino's effect on India .
Other teleconnections

NAO (North Atlantic Oscillation): pressure see-saw between the Azores High and the Icelandic Low, affecting European winters. MJO (Madden-Julian Oscillation): an eastward-moving pulse of rain with a 30-60 day cycle that causes active and break spells in the monsoon. Arctic Oscillation : affects cold air outbreaks.
How agencies track it

The Oceanic Nino Index (ONI) uses the Nino 3.4 region sea temperature anomaly. An anomaly of +0.5 degrees C or more for several months signals El Nino. The IOD is measured by the Dipole Mode Index, the difference between the west and east boxes. IMD and NOAA publish forecasts, and IMD uses ENSO and IOD in its monsoon outlook.
Effects on India

El Nino years such as 2009, 2014, 2015 and 2023 had deficient or erratic monsoon rainfall. Kharif output and food prices can be hit. La Nina years often bring floods in Assam and Bihar. The government watches ENSO to plan buffer stocks, export curbs and relief. These patterns change; check the latest IMD outlook before the exam.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Explain El Nino and its impact on India', 'What is the Indian Ocean Dipole and how does it influence the monsoon?', 'What is a teleconnection?' Draw the Pacific with normal and El Nino flows. Give the IOD as a second layer and mention 1997 and 2019. Close with economic effects: food prices, power demand, hydro output.
Ocean Relief, Temperature and Salinity
The oceans cover 71% of Earth

Fisheries, oil, minerals, trade routes and climate all depend on the ocean floor, its temperature and its salt. India has a coastline of about 11,098 km including islands (re-measured in 2025) and an Exclusive Economic Zone of about 2 million sq km.
The shape of the ocean floor
Most ocean floor is the abyssal plain, covered with deep mud called ooze . Sediment thins away from the coast.
Ridges, seamounts and trenches

Mid-ocean ridges are underwater mountain chains where plates diverge (Mid-Atlantic Ridge). Seamounts are submerged volcanoes; flat-topped ones are guyots . Trenches are mostly in the Pacific; the Mariana Trench, with Challenger Deep at about 11 km, is the deepest known point. Mid-ocean ridges plus deep trenches make the "Ring of Fire" in the Pacific.
Coral reefs

Corals need warm clear water of 20-30 C, sunlight and salinity near 35 ppt, so they grow in shallow tropical seas, mostly between 30 N and 30 S, away from muddy river mouths. Types: fringing (touching land), barrier (lagoon between; Great Barrier Reef, the largest) and atoll (ring around a lagoon; Lakshadweep). Coral bleaching occurs when warm water makes corals expel their algae. India's reefs: Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep.
Ocean temperature

Sea surface temperature falls from about 27 C near the equator to near freezing at the poles. It is highest slightly north of the equator because land in the north holds heat. Warm currents raise temperature, cold ones lower it. In the north, enclosed seas can be warmer (Red Sea) and Arctic seas colder. Temperature falls with depth to near 0 to 4 C.
Salinity

Salinity is grams of salt per kilogram of seawater, about 35 on average. It rises with evaporation and falls with rain, river inflow and melting ice. Highest in the tropics (20-30 degrees), lower at the equator (rain) and at the poles (melt).
Why salinity matters

Salinity and temperature set the density of water. Dense water sinks and drives the deep thermohaline circulation , the "ocean conveyor belt" that moves heat around the planet. Freshwater from melting ice can weaken this circulation: a concern for Atlantic currents.
Ocean warming and deep-sea mining

The oceans absorb over 90% of the excess heat of global warming. Marine heatwaves kill coral and fish. Meanwhile countries race for polymetallic nodules (nickel, cobalt, manganese) on the deep seabed. Supporters see critical minerals for batteries. Critics fear unknown damage to deep ecosystems. The International Seabed Authority (ISA) is still writing rules.
The Indian Ocean floor and resources

Features: the Chagos-Laccadive Ridge (Lakshadweep sits on it), the Ninety East Ridge , and the Andaman-Nicobar ridge. India holds an ISA licence for about 75,000 sq km in the Central Indian Ocean Basin for nodules. The Deep Ocean Mission (2021) includes the Samudrayaan manned submersible project.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the factors affecting the salinity of ocean water." (10 marks) "Why does the Bay of Bengal have lower salinity than the Arabian Sea?" (10 marks) Structure: list the zones of relief with an unusual feature; factors of temperature and salinity; end with resources and India's programmes. Prelims tip: average salinity is 35 ppt; the Dead Sea is the saltiest; trenches are mostly in the Pacific.
Currents, Tides and Ocean Resources
Moving water shapes trade and climate

Currents decide where deserts, fog and fisheries occur. Tides decide when ships can enter ports. The sea also supplies fish, oil, gas and minerals. These are core topics for GS I and for the blue economy theme in current affairs.
What drives currents

Currents are large streams of water. Drivers: prevailing winds , Coriolis force , differences in temperature and salinity (density), gravity and coastlines. Currents flow clockwise in the northern gyres and anticlockwise in the southern.
Warm and cold currents

Warm currents flow from low to high latitudes. Cold currents flow towards the equator, usually along west coasts. Where they meet, as off Newfoundland, fog forms and plankton thrives, making rich fisheries (Grand Banks, Japan, North Sea).
Effects of currents on climate

The North Atlantic Drift keeps north-west European ports like Bergen ice-free. Cold currents along west coasts cut rainfall and form coastal deserts : Atacama and Namib. The Humboldt current is linked to El Nino collapses in Peru's anchovy fishery.
Indian Ocean: currents that reverse

Unlike the Atlantic and Pacific, the northern Indian Ocean has seasonally reversing currents, driven by the monsoon. In summer, the South-West Monsoon Drift flows eastward. In winter, the North-East Monsoon Drift flows westward. South of 10 S the circulation is a steady anticlockwise gyre. Hence ancient sailors used the monsoon to cross.
Tides
Tides come from the Moon's and Sun's gravity and Earth's spin. Narrow, funnel-shaped bays raise the range: the Bay of Fundy (about 16 m) is the highest. Tide energy and port design use these data.
Ocean resources

Living: fish, seaweed. Mineral: salt, magnesium, nodules, sand. Energy: oil and gas (Mumbai High), tidal and wave power, gas hydrates . The Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, 1982) gives a 12 nautical mile territorial sea, a 200 nautical mile EEZ , and rights to the extended continental shelf.
Blue economy: growth or damage?

The ocean may be a new growth engine, but overfishing, plastic and bottom trawling threaten it. The Gulf Stream-linked AMOC may be slowing due to meltwater, which could shift weather in Europe and monsoon patterns. Science is still unsure about timing.
India's tides and blue economy

India has large tides in the Gulf of Khambhat and the Gulf of Kutch (up to about 11 m at Kandla); both are tidal power sites. The Hooghly sees a tidal bore. India is among the top fish producers, second only to China, with about 9% of world aquatic production (FAO, 2026). Sagarmala develops ports; the Deep Ocean Mission (2021) and a Blue Economy policy frame the push. Mumbai High remains the largest offshore oil field.
How to write this

Likely questions "Describe the ocean currents of the Indian Ocean and how they differ from those of the Atlantic." (10 marks) "How do ocean currents influence the climate of coastal areas?" (10 marks) Structure: causes; examples in a table; effects (rain, fog, fisheries); Indian Ocean reversal; end with policy. Prelims tip: cold currents on west coasts of continents at 15-30 degrees; spring tides occur at new and full moon; EEZ is 200 nm.
Coral Reefs, Atolls and Marine Ecosystems
Reefs are small in area but huge in life

Coral reefs cover under 1 percent of the ocean floor but shelter about a quarter of marine species. They protect coasts and feed millions. They are under threat from warming seas. UPSC asks about reef types, Darwin's theory, bleaching and Indian reefs.
What is a coral reef?

Corals are tiny animals called polyps . They build hard skeletons of calcium carbonate. Inside their tissue live algae called zooxanthellae , which give colour and food through photosynthesis. Reef corals need clear, shallow, warm water: 20 to 30 degrees C, salinity of about 32 to 36 parts per thousand, depth under about 50 m, and sunlight. They do not grow near river mouths, where fresh and muddy water harms them.
Three types of reef

Fringing reef : grows right against the shore, with a shallow, narrow lagoon or none. Common round Andaman islands. Barrier reef : separated from land by a wide, deep lagoon. The Great Barrier Reef is the largest. Atoll : a ring of coral enclosing a lagoon, with no central land. Lakshadweep and the Maldives are mostly atolls.
Darwin's subsidence theory

Charles Darwin (1842, The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs ) proposed that a fringing reef grows around a volcanic island. As the island slowly sinks, the coral grows upward to stay near light. The reef becomes a barrier reef, then an atoll when the island vanishes. Drilling at Eniwetok atoll in the 1950s found volcanic rock beneath over a kilometre of coral, supporting Darwin.
Other theories

Daly's glacial control theory : sea level fell in the ice age, planing islands flat; rising seas then let coral grow upward. Murray's theory: reefs build on submarine platforms. Today most geologists accept a mix: subsidence plus sea-level change.
Where the big reefs are

The Great Barrier Reef (about 2,300 km, Queensland, Australia) is the largest. The Belize Barrier Reef is the biggest in the Atlantic. Atolls are common in the Maldives, Lakshadweep, Marshall Islands and Tuvalu. Reefs lie mainly between 30 degrees N and S in the Indo-Pacific and the Caribbean.
Coral bleaching

When water gets too warm, corals expel their algae and turn white. They are not dead but starving. If the heat persists, they die. The Great Barrier Reef suffered mass bleaching in 1998, 2002, 2016, 2017, 2020 and 2022. Other threats: ocean acidification (absorbing CO2 weakens skeletons), crown-of-thorns starfish, destructive fishing, and sediment runoff.
Other marine ecosystems

Mangroves grow in salty tidal mud and shelter fish nurseries. Seagrass meadows feed dugongs and turtles. Estuaries mix river and sea water and are among the most productive zones. Upwelling zones (Peru, Namibia, Somalia) are rich in plankton and fish. Deep-sea vents run on chemical energy rather than sunlight. The photic zone , the top 200 m or so, holds most marine life because light reaches it. Phytoplankton there make about half of the oxygen we breathe.
India's reefs

Four main reef areas: Gulf of Mannar (Tamil Nadu), Gulf of Kachchh (Gujarat), Lakshadweep (atolls) and Andaman and Nicobar (fringing reefs). Gulf of Mannar was declared a biosphere reserve in 1989, the first marine one in South and Southeast Asia. Coral is also protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Explain the types of coral reef and the conditions for growth', 'Discuss Darwin's theory', 'Causes and effects of coral bleaching'. List the conditions in five bullets. Draw fringing, barrier and atoll in one line each. End with conservation: marine protected areas, reducing emissions, coral restoration.
Mid-Ocean Ridges, Trenches and Marine Deposits
The sea floor is not flat

The ocean floor has mountains longer than any on land, trenches deeper than Everest is tall, and sediments that record Earth's history. These features prove plate tectonics and decide where earthquakes, volcanoes and tsunamis occur. They are a favourite topic in prelims and in questions on map work.
Four zones of ocean relief

Continental shelf : gently sloping, up to about 200 m deep, rich in fish and oil. Continental slope : steep drop to the deep sea, cut by submarine canyons. Abyssal plain : flat floor at 3,000 to 6,000 m. Ocean deeps (trenches) : narrow, below 6,000 m. The average ocean depth is about 3,700 m.
Mid-ocean ridges

A mid-ocean ridge is an underwater mountain chain along a divergent plate boundary. Magma rises, cools and forms new crust. The system runs about 65,000 km, the longest mountain chain on Earth. Examples: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge , the East Pacific Rise and the Carlsberg Ridge in the Indian Ocean. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge cuts through Iceland, where it rises above sea level.
Sea-floor spreading

Harry Hess proposed the idea in 1960-62. Robert Dietz named it. New crust forms at the ridge and moves away on both sides. Vine and Matthews (1963) found magnetic stripes in matching patterns on each side of the ridge. They recorded reversals of Earth's magnetic field. This was strong proof. Sea-floor rocks are young: none older than about 200 million years, because old crust is destroyed in trenches.
Ocean trenches

Trenches are deep, narrow troughs at subduction zones , where one plate dives under another. The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific has the deepest point, Challenger Deep, about 10,900 m below sea level. Most trenches lie in the Pacific, around the Ring of Fire . Other deep trenches: Tonga, Kuril-Kamchatka, Philippine, Java (Sunda), Puerto Rico in the Atlantic.
Other sea-floor features

Seamounts : underwater volcanoes that do not reach the surface. Guyots : flat-topped seamounts. Submarine canyons : cut by turbidity currents (the Hudson canyon). Oceanic plateaus : the Chagos-Laccadive ridge and the Kerguelen Plateau. Volcanic islands: Hawaii, Iceland, Reunion. Iceland sits on both a ridge and a hot spot.
Marine deposits

Sediments settle slowly on the sea floor. Terrigenous deposits come from land (mud, sand) and lie near the shore. Pelagic deposits are from the open sea. They include oozes (from shells of tiny organisms: calcareous ooze above the carbonate compensation depth, siliceous ooze below) and red clay (very fine, deepest basins). Volcanic deposits come from eruptions.
Ocean resources on the floor

Polymetallic nodules hold manganese, nickel, cobalt and copper. The Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the Pacific is the best known. Hydrothermal vents deposit sulphides. Gas hydrates store methane in cold sediments. The International Seabed Authority (Kingston, Jamaica, under UNCLOS 1982) regulates seabed mining beyond national waters.
India's ocean floor

The Carlsberg Ridge , Central Indian Ridge and Southwest Indian Ridge mark the Indian Ocean spreading system. India holds exploration rights for nodules in the Central Indian Ocean Basin and sulphides on the Carlsberg and Indian Ridges, granted by the ISA. The Deep Ocean Mission (2021) and the Samudrayaan submersible Matsya 6000 support this.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Evidence for sea-floor spreading', 'Why are trenches in the Pacific?', 'Importance of polymetallic nodules'. For evidence: magnetic stripes, young crust, ridge heat flow, drilling ages. Draw a ridge and a trench with arrows showing crust born and crust destroyed. Link nodules to India's critical mineral needs and to the Deep Ocean Mission.
Soils and Natural Vegetation of the World
Soil and plants tie climate to people

Soil decides what farmers can grow. Vegetation decides what animals and people can live there. Together with climate they give every region its character. UPSC asks for distribution and reasons : why laterite in the tropics, why chernozem in the steppes.
Soil: how it forms

Pedogenesis depends on five factors: parent material , climate , relief , organisms and time . Climate is the most active. Warm, wet climates cause fast chemical weathering; cold or dry ones cause slow formation. Soil is a living system, 45% mineral, 25% water, 25% air and 5% organic matter, roughly.
The soil profile
A vertical cut through soil is a profile . The A horizon is the most fertile. Leaching washes nutrients down; eluviation and illuviation move clay and iron from upper layers to the B horizon.
Zonal soils of the world
Laterite (Latin later, brick) forms by laterisation : silica leaches, iron and aluminium remain. Hardens on exposure, so it is used for bricks, as in Kerala and Karnataka.
Natural vegetation: the biomes
Natural vegetation grows without human help. Temperature, moisture, soil and relief decide its type. With height, vegetation changes like it does with latitude: altitudinal zonation .
Tropical and Mediterranean forests

Equatorial rainforest : evergreen, layered, rich in species. Hardwoods like mahogany and ebony, hard to harvest. Monsoon forests shed leaves in the dry season: teak, sal. Savanna : tall grass and scattered trees. Mediterranean vegetation has small, waxy, drought-proof leaves: olives, citrus and vines. These regions are the world's citrus and wine orchards, called "orchards of the world".
Grasslands, taiga and tundra

Temperate grasslands are among the world's great wheat and cattle regions. Taiga is coniferous (pine, spruce, fir) with softwood for paper and matches. Tundra has mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs on permafrost; reindeer are central to the ecosystem.
Is soil a renewable resource?

Soil forms at a few centimetres per thousand years but erodes in decades if bare. Deforestation, over-grazing and chemical farming cause degradation and desertification. The UN Convention to Combat Desertification ( UNCCD , 1994) works on this. The debate: grow more food now, or protect the slow-forming soil base for the future? India's answer includes Soil Health Cards (2015) and watershed programmes.
India's soils and vegetation

India's main soil types: alluvial, black (regur), red, laterite, arid and forest soils. Black soil comes from Deccan basalt and suits cotton. Laterite is in the Western Ghats and east coast. Natural vegetation ranges from Western Ghats rainforest to Thar scrub and Himalayan alpine meadows (more in the Indian lessons). India lost some forest in the Himalaya and Northeast through jhum and mining, but the Forest Survey of India reports slow net gains in cover (as of ISFR 2023).
How to write this

Likely questions "Explain the process of laterisation and its effect on the soils of tropical regions." (10 marks) "Why are temperate grasslands called the granaries of the world?" (10 marks) Structure: climate first, then soil, then vegetation, then human use. Prelims tip: match grasslands to their continents (pampas = Argentina, veld = South Africa, downs = Australia); chernozems are black earths of the steppe.
Biomes of the World
Climate draws the map of life

A biome is a large community of plants and animals shaped by climate. Temperature and rainfall decide which biome sits where. UPSC asks about forests, grasslands and deserts with their examples, adaptations and threats. It also links to climate change, because biomes are shifting.
The big picture

Land biomes: tropical rainforest, tropical savanna, desert, temperate grassland, Mediterranean scrub, temperate deciduous forest, taiga (boreal forest) and tundra. Moving from the equator to the poles, the temperature falls and the plant forms change from broad-leaf evergreen to needle-leaf to moss and lichen.
Tropical rainforest

Within 10 degrees of the equator. Rain above 2,000 mm, no dry season, 25-27 degrees C. Layers: emergent, canopy, understory, forest floor. Very high diversity, thin soils that leach and lose nutrients. Found in the Amazon, Congo, and Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia). Forest loss through logging, palm oil and cattle is the main threat.
Savanna and temperate grasslands

Savanna : grass with scattered trees, wet and dry seasons. East Africa (Serengeti), Brazil's Campos and Llanos. Big herds and predators. Temperate grasslands : fewer trees, cold winters, fertile dark soil. Prairies (North America), Pampas (Argentina), Steppes (Eurasia), Veld (South Africa), Downs (Australia). These are the world's wheat belts.
Deserts

Under 250 mm of rain. Hot deserts: Sahara, Arabian, Thar, Australian. Cold deserts: Gobi, Patagonia, Ladakh. Plants (xerophytes) have thick stems, waxy leaves, spines, deep roots (cactus, acacia). Animals are nocturnal or store water. Deserts form in the subtropical high pressure belts, in rain shadows (Atacama) and in continental interiors (Gobi).
Mediterranean and temperate forests

Mediterranean : hot, dry summer and mild, wet winter, between 30 and 40 degrees on west coasts. Evergreen shrubs, citrus, olive and vines. California, central Chile, southwest Australia, the Cape. Temperate deciduous : four seasons, trees shed leaves (oak, beech, maple). Eastern USA, western Europe, northeast China. Much cleared for farming.
Taiga and tundra

Taiga (boreal forest): the largest land biome, across Canada, Scandinavia and Siberia. Conifers (spruce, fir, pine) with needles that shed snow. Long winters, thin acidic podzol soils, lumber and pulp. Tundra : treeless, permafrost, mosses and lichens, short summer. Arctic tundra stores huge carbon; thawing releases methane and CO2.
Are biome boundaries fixed?

No. Warming is pushing the tree line upward in mountains and northward in the Arctic. Rainforest in the Amazon may tip to savanna under drought and deforestation, a possible tipping point discussed by scientists such as Carlos Nobre. Some biologists prefer the term ecoregion because boundaries are fuzzy and local variety matters.
Biomes in India

India has rainforest (Western Ghats, northeast, Andaman), savanna-like tropical dry deciduous forest, thorn scrub (Rajasthan, Gujarat), desert (Thar, Ladakh cold desert), mangroves (Sundarbans), and alpine meadows and tundra above the tree line in the Himalaya. Temperate grassland is limited to alpine pastures like the Bugyals of Uttarakhand.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Compare savanna and temperate grasslands', 'Why are tropical rainforest soils poor despite lush growth?', 'Impact of climate change on biomes'. Use a table: location, climate, vegetation, soil, human use, threat. Give local names (Pampas, Veld, Steppe) with the continent. For soils: fast nutrient cycling in the plants, not the soil.
Biogeographic Realms and Biodiversity Hotspots
Where life is rich, and where it is at risk

Biogeography asks why species live where they do. Hotspot ideas guide conservation money and policy. UPSC mixes this with environment: 'Which of these is a hotspot?' and 'Why is the Western Ghats a hotspot?' appear again and again.
Wallace's realms

Alfred Russel Wallace (1876, The Geographical Distribution of Animals ) divided the land into zoogeographic regions: Nearctic , Neotropical , Palaearctic , Ethiopian (Afrotropical), Oriental (Indomalayan) and Australasian . Realms differ because continents were separated for long periods, which let unique species evolve.
Wallace Line and island biogeography

Wallace noticed that animals differ sharply across a narrow strait between Bali and Lombok. West of it, Asian animals; east of it, Australian types like marsupials. This is the Wallace Line . MacArthur and Wilson (1967, The Theory of Island Biogeography ) showed that bigger, nearer islands hold more species. This idea guides the design of reserves.
Endemism and speciation

A species is endemic if found nowhere else. Islands and isolated mountains hold many. Adaptive radiation : one ancestor splits into many forms (Darwin's finches in the Galapagos). Convergent evolution : unrelated species look alike in similar habitats (sharks and dolphins). Madagascar split from India and Africa and holds lemurs found nowhere else.
The hotspot concept

Norman Myers proposed it in 1988. Conservation International later fixed the criteria: at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species (0.5 percent of the world total) and at least 70 percent of the original habitat lost . Hotspots cover about 2.5 percent of land but hold over half of the world's endemic plant species.
How many hotspots?

The count was 25 in 2000, 34 in 2005, and 36 now after the addition of the North American Coastal Plain in 2016 and the Forests of East Australia in 2017. Examples: Tropical Andes, Mesoamerica, Caribbean, Atlantic Forest, Cerrado, Mediterranean Basin, Madagascar, Cape Floristic Region, Sundaland, Wallacea, Philippines, Japan.
Megadiverse countries

Seventeen countries hold most of the world's species. The list includes Brazil, Colombia, Indonesia, China, Mexico, Peru, Ecuador, Venezuela, USA, Australia, Madagascar, South Africa, DR Congo, Philippines, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea and India . India has about 7-8 percent of recorded species on 2.4 percent of the land.
India's hotspots

India has four: the Himalaya , the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka , Indo-Burma (northeast India) and Sundaland (the Nicobar Islands). The Western Ghats are older than the Himalaya, rich in endemics such as the Nilgiri tahr and lion-tailed macaque, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2012.
Hotspots or whole landscapes?

Critics say hotspots miss places rich in species but not threatened, such as the high-forest Amazon, and may ignore ecosystem services. Others support them as a clear, cheap way to rank priorities. Some conservationists prefer global 200 ecoregions or key biodiversity areas .
How to answer

Likely questions: 'What are biodiversity hotspots? Why is the Western Ghats one?', 'Criteria for hotspots', 'Which Indian regions are part of hotspots?' Give two criteria and the Myers date. Name four Indian hotspots with their states. Finish with threats: habitat loss, invasive species, mining, linear infrastructure.
Himalayas, Northern Plains and Peninsular Plateau
India's relief explains its climate, rivers, soils and wars

The Himalaya block cold winds and trap the monsoon. The plains feed 1.4 billion people. The plateau holds India's minerals. Almost every Indian geography answer starts with these three. Questions often ask for comparisons and reasons .
Six physiographic divisions
Physiography means the study of landforms. India's land area is about 3.28 million sq km. It spans 8 degrees 4 minutes N to 37 degrees 6 minutes N on the mainland.
The Himalaya: three parallel ranges
They are young fold mountains , about 2,400 km long, arched in a curve from the Indus gorge to the Dihang gorge. Each range has a different rock age and origin.
Himalayan divisions

Himadri holds Everest, Kanchenjunga (the highest peak in India, 8,586 m) and the glaciers. Himachal : Pir Panjal, Dhauladhar, Mussoorie, with hill stations and Kashmir valley. Shiwaliks : loose gravel and sandstone, with long valleys called duns (Dehradun) in Uttarakhand and duars in the east. By river (Sidney Burrard): Punjab (Indus to Sutlej), Kumaon (Sutlej to Kali), Nepal (Kali to Tista), Assam (Tista to Dihang).
The Northern Plains

Built by alluvium from the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra, about 7 lakh sq km. Divisions: Punjab-Haryana plain, Ganga plain, Brahmaputra plain. The plain slopes gently, and rivers form meanders , braided channels , and levees . Frequent floods go with high fertility.
The Peninsular Plateau

This is the oldest and most stable block, a part of Gondwanaland . The Narmada-Tapi flow in rift valleys, westwards. The Chotanagpur plateau is the mineral heartland. The Western Ghats are a block mountain edge, and rains to the west are heavy.
Gaps, passes and shape

Western Ghats gaps: Thal (Mumbai-Nashik), Bhor (Mumbai-Pune), Pal (Kerala-Tamil Nadu). Himalayan passes: Shipki La, Nathu La, Zoji La, Banihal, Rohtang, Jelep La. Mountain passes matter for trade and for military moves along the northern border.
Developing a fragile mountain

Himalayan roads, tunnels and hydropower bring jobs and security. Yet Joshimath sank in 2023, and the Uttarkashi Silkyara tunnel collapse (November 2023) and the 2013 Kedarnath and 2021 Chamoli floods show the risk. The Char Dham road debate pitted defence needs against ecology; the Supreme Court allowed a wider road in 2021 for the border.
Why the plains matter, and why the Himalaya shield

The Himalaya turn the monsoon back, so the Gangetic plains get rain, and they shield India from cold Central Asian winds. Glaciers feed the perennial rivers. The plains produce a large share of wheat and rice, and have about 40% of India's people. The Western Ghats are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012) and a biodiversity hotspot. The Himalaya are a hotspot too.
How to write this

Likely questions "Describe the physiographic divisions of India and their significance." (15 marks) "Himalayan range is vast and complex. Discuss how each range differs." (10 marks) Structure: list divisions; a short paragraph with key features and a number each; one line on economic or climatic significance; a current example. Prelims tip: Kanchenjunga is India's highest peak; Anamudi is the highest peak south of the Himalaya; Narmada flows west through a rift valley.
Coasts, Islands and Drainage Systems
Rivers, ports and islands

Rivers carry 1.4 billion people's water. Coasts carry 95% of India's trade by volume. Islands give India a strategic reach in the Indian Ocean. Questions mix physical facts (west-flowing rivers) with policy (rivers, ports, islands).
Western and eastern coasts

The east coast has big deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. The west coast has estuaries (Narmada, Tapi) because rivers cut straight, short courses to the sea. India's mainland coastline is about 6,100 km; with islands it is about 7,516 km (older figure). A re-measurement released in 2025 raised it to about 11,098 km, without any new land: modern mapping simply traces the coast in finer detail.
Lagoons, lakes and backwaters

Chilika (Odisha) is the largest coastal lagoon in India and the largest brackish lagoon in Asia, a Ramsar site. Pulicat sits on the Andhra-Tamil Nadu border. Kerala's kayals (Vembanad, Ashtamudi) are tourist backwaters. Sand bars separate them from the sea.
The islands

Lakshadweep: 32 sq km, separated from the Maldives by the Eight Degree channel and Minicoy by the Nine Degree channel. Andaman and Nicobar: about 570 islands, divided by the Ten Degree Channel . Narcondam is dormant; Barren Island is active. Islands matter as a strategic outpost near the Malacca Strait.
Two river systems
Antecedent means the river kept its course as the Himalaya rose. Peninsular rivers follow the slope.
The three big Himalayan rivers

Indus : from near Mansarovar, enters India in Ladakh, joined by the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. Ganga : Bhagirathi from Gangotri meets the Alaknanda at Devprayag. Tributaries: Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi, Son. Brahmaputra : from Tibet (Tsangpo), enters India as the Dihang, and flows through Assam.
Peninsular rivers and patterns
Godavari is the longest (about 1,465 km), called Dakshin Ganga. Krishna and Kaveri are vital for farming. The Narmada and Tapi flow west in rift valleys.
River management and cooperation

Brahmaputra dams in Tibet (China's Medog project, approved in December 2024) worry India about flows. The Indus Waters Treaty (1960) was held in abeyance by India in April 2025 after the Pahalgam attack. Within India, states fight over the Kaveri, Krishna and Godavari. Experts argue for basin-level planning.
Ganga and its cleaning

Ganga basin is about 26% of India's land and supports about 40% of its people. Namami Gange , started in 2014 under NMCG, built sewage plants. Ganga was declared the national river in 2008. The Ganga river dolphin is the national aquatic animal. The east coast's deltas are cyclone-prone. The west coast's estuaries (Narmada, Tapi) hold major ports like Surat and Hazira.
How to write this

Likely questions "Compare the east-flowing and west-flowing peninsular rivers." (10 marks) "Explain the strategic importance of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands." (10 marks) Structure: table-style comparison; reasons for the difference (gradient, rift valley); then a current issue (water sharing, ports). Prelims tip: know the channels (Eight, Nine, Ten Degree), Indira Point, Chilika, the Kaveri as a perennial-ish river with two monsoons, and that Godavari is the longest peninsular river.
Himalayan Divisions, Passes and Glaciers
A favourite for map and fact questions

The Himalaya appear in prelims through peaks, passes, glaciers and ranges, and in mains through hazards, rivers and strategy. This lesson goes beyond the basic three ranges to give the regional pattern, the key passes and the glaciers you must recall.
Trans-Himalaya and the high peaks

North of the Great Himalaya lies the Trans-Himalaya : the Karakoram, Ladakh and Zaskar ranges. The Karakoram holds K2 (8,611 m), the world's second highest peak, now in Pakistan-administered territory. Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) on the Sikkim-Nepal border is the highest peak in India. Nanda Devi (7,816 m) is the highest peak lying wholly within India.
Regional divisions

Sidney Burrard divided the Himalaya by rivers: Punjab Himalaya (Indus to Satluj), Kumaon Himalaya (Satluj to Kali), Nepal Himalaya (Kali to Tista) and Assam Himalaya (Tista to Dihang). Beyond the Dihang, the Purvanchal hills (Patkai, Naga, Manipur, Mizo) turn south.
Lesser Himalaya ranges and valleys

Pir Panjal is the longest range of the Lesser Himalaya. Others: Dhauladhar, Nag Tibba, Mussoorie and Mahabharat. The Kashmir valley lies between the Pir Panjal and the Great Himalaya. Other valleys: Kangra and Kullu. Hill stations include Shimla, Mussoorie, Nainital and Darjeeling. Between the Lesser Himalaya and the Shiwalik are the duns , such as Dehradun.
Key mountain passes

Banihal (Pir Panjal): Jammu to Srinagar, with the Jawahar tunnel. Zoji La : Srinagar to Leh, on the Great Himalaya. Khardung La : Leh to Nubra valley, among the world's highest motorable roads. Nathu La and Jelep La : Sikkim to Tibet. Shipki La : Himachal Pradesh to Tibet; the Satluj enters India here. Lipulekh and Niti : Uttarakhand to Tibet. Bomdi La and Dihang in Arunachal Pradesh. Rohtang in Himachal; the Atal Tunnel (2020) passes below it.
Glaciers

The Himalaya hold the largest ice outside the poles, called the 'Third Pole'. Siachen (about 70 km, Karakoram, Nubra river source). Gangotri (about 30 km, source of the Bhagirathi, whose snout is at Gaumukh). Zemu (Sikkim, Kanchenjunga). Pindari , Milam (Kumaon). Baltoro and Biafo are in Pakistan-administered Karakoram. Kolahoi is in Kashmir.
Snow line and glacier types

The snow line is the height above which snow stays all year. It lies near 4,500-6,000 m in the Himalaya, lower on the wet eastern side. Himalayan glaciers are mostly valley glaciers . A cirque glacier sits in an armchair hollow. A piedmont glacier spreads at the foot of a mountain. India's cold desert in Ladakh sits in the rain shadow of the Great Himalaya.
Retreat, GLOFs and the cryosphere

ICIMOD's 2023 Hindu Kush Himalaya report found that glaciers are melting faster than in earlier decades. A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) hit Kedarnath in 2013 and South Lhonak lake in Sikkim in October 2023. The Chamoli disaster of February 2021 was a rock-ice avalanche. Scientists still debate how much loss is due to warming and how much to black carbon.
Strategy and ecology

Passes shape border trade and defence: Nathu La reopened for trade with China in 2006. Roads and tunnels such as the Atal Tunnel and Zojila tunnel project improve all-weather access. The Himalaya are also a water tower for the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra, so glacier change is a food and energy security issue.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Himalayan glaciers and climate change', 'Strategic significance of passes', 'Regional divisions of the Himalaya'. Match each pass to a state and a neighbour country. Use a labelled outline map: Pir Panjal, Zaskar, Karakoram, Purvanchal. For glaciers: causes, risks (GLOFs, flood, drought) and responses (early warning, hydropower rules).
Northern Plains: Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar and Khadar
India's food bowl has an internal order

The northern plains cover about 7 lakh sq km and feed hundreds of millions. They are not uniform. They vary in soil, drainage and flood risk from the foothills to the river. UPSC often asks for the sequence and the contrast between old and new alluvium.
Origin

The plains are made of alluvium from the Himalayan rivers, laid in a deep trough (a foredeep) formed in front of the rising Himalaya. Depth of deposits is thousands of metres in places. The plains extend about 3,200 km from the Indus delta to the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta.
Bhabar
A narrow belt, 8-16 km wide, along the foot of the Shiwalik. Rivers drop pebbles and boulders here. The coarse deposit is so porous that streams sink and disappear . It suits large trees, not crops.
Terai

South of the Bhabar, the lost streams re-emerge in a damp, marshy belt, 15-30 km wide. It was dense forest with wildlife, much now cleared for farming (sugarcane, rice, wheat in Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand). Malaria used to be a problem. Dudhwa and Corbett lie on this belt.
Bhangar
Older alluvium. It forms the higher terraces, beyond flood reach. Often dark with lime nodules called kankar . Soils are rich but less renewed. Found away from the river channels.
Khadar
Newer alluvium in the active floodplain. Fine silt, light-coloured, replenished by yearly floods. Very fertile and ideal for rice, jute, vegetables. Floods are the cost of fertility.
Bhangar vs Khadar

Age : Bhangar is older (Pleistocene), Khadar is newer (Holocene). Position : higher terraces vs lower floodplain. Fertility : lower in Bhangar, higher in Khadar. Kankar : present in Bhangar, absent in Khadar. Flooding : Bhangar is safe, Khadar floods often. Also remember reh or kallar : salt-affected soils, common in Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.
Regional pattern

Four sub-regions by rivers: Punjab plains (doabs between five rivers, mostly irrigated), Ganga plains (Haryana to West Bengal; includes the Ganga-Yamuna doab), Brahmaputra plains (Assam, with many river islands like Majuli) and Rajasthan plain , the Thar. Rainfall drops westward, from over 150 cm in the east to under 50 cm in the west.
Floods, rice and wheat

The plains hold the Green Revolution core (Punjab, Haryana, west UP). Bihar's Kosi, called the 'Sorrow of Bihar', shifted course by about 120 km over two centuries and flooded severely in 2008 after the Kusaha breach. Groundwater depletion in Punjab and Haryana is a serious concern, as shown by NASA GRACE data in 2009.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Differentiate Bhangar and Khadar', 'Describe the physiographic features of the northern plains', 'Why are the plains densely populated?' Use a cross-section from foothills to river: Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar, Khadar. Give a one-line fact per zone. Link soil and water to crop patterns and population density.
Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats and the Deccan Plateau
The plateau shapes rivers, rain and minerals
