The Peninsular plateau is among the oldest landmasses on Earth. It holds minerals, black soil and the ghat escarpments that catch the monsoon. UPSC asks for comparisons of the two Ghats and for how the plateau's relief controls rivers.
Structure of the plateau

A tilted tableland of ancient crystalline rock from Gondwana times. It slopes east , so major peninsular rivers flow to the Bay of Bengal. Subdivisions: Central Highlands (Malwa plateau, Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand), Deccan Plateau (Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana), Chotanagpur Plateau (Jharkhand, mineral-rich), and the northeastern extension (Meghalaya Plateau).
Deccan Trap

Northwest Deccan is covered by basalt from huge fissure eruptions about 66 million years ago, near the end of the Cretaceous. These lavas weather into regur (black) soil. The Deccan eruptions have been linked with the dinosaur extinction, along with the Chicxulub impact in Mexico.
Western Ghats (Sahyadri)

Run parallel to the west coast for about 1,600 km from the Tapi to Kanyakumari. Continuous, steep on the western side, broken only by the Palghat Gap . Higher peaks: Anai Mudi (2,695 m, Kerala, highest in peninsula), Doddabetta in the Nilgiris. Passes: Thal Ghat, Bhor Ghat, Palghat. They cause heavy orographic rain on the windward side.
Eastern Ghats

Broken, discontinuous hills along the east coast, cut by the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. Highest point Mahendragiri (about 1,501 m, Odisha) or Jindhagada Peak (about 1,690 m, Andhra) depending on the source. Lower and older than the Western Ghats. They meet the Western Ghats at the Nilgiris .
Western vs Eastern Ghats

Continuity : Western continuous, Eastern broken by rivers. Height : Western averages about 900-1,600 m; Eastern about 600 m. Rainfall : Western heavy; the Eastern side gets less. Rivers : Western Ghats are the source of the Godavari and Krishna; Eastern are cut through by them. Forests : Western moist evergreen; Eastern deciduous.
Hills of the plateau

Aravalli : oldest fold mountain, Guru Shikhar (Mt Abu, 1,722 m) is the highest. Vindhya and Satpura form the divide between north and peninsular India; the Narmada lies between them. Mahadeo hills and Pachmarhi in Madhya Pradesh. Nilgiri hills hold Ooty. Cardamom and Palani hills in the south. Rajmahal hills in Jharkhand.
Western Ghats: protection vs development

The Gadgil Committee (2011) proposed to treat the whole range as ecologically sensitive, with three zones. The Kasturirangan Committee (2013) reduced it to about 37 percent of the area. States resisted because of mining, dams and plantations. The Wayanad landslide of July 2024 revived the debate.
Minerals and rivers

The plateau holds most of India's coal, iron ore, manganese, mica and bauxite, especially in the Chotanagpur belt. Rivers such as the Godavari and Krishna start in the west and flow east through the plateau. The Narmada and Tapi flow west through rift valleys.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Compare the Western and Eastern Ghats', 'Importance of the Western Ghats', 'Why do most peninsular rivers flow east?' Use a comparison table: length, height, continuity, rain, vegetation, passes. Mention the Palghat Gap and the Nilgiri junction. For rivers: tilt of the plateau and the west coast rift-fault.
Thar Desert, Coastal Plains and Island Groups
The edges of India

The Thar, the two coastal plains and the island groups complete the physiography. These regions are often tested through coast names, deltas and islands in the news. Learn the names in sequence along the coast.
Thar Desert

Lies west of the Aravalli, mainly in Rajasthan and extending to Gujarat, Haryana and Pakistan. Rain under 25 cm. Features: barchans , longitudinal dunes , playas (salt lakes: Sambhar, Didwana, Pachpadra), and the seasonal Luni , which ends in the Rann of Kachchh. Once a sea bed; dried over geological time. The old Saraswati is thought to have flowed nearby.
Western coastal plain

Narrow (10-25 km), between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea, from Gujarat to Kerala. Parts: Konkan (Mumbai to Goa), Karnataka (Kanara) coast , Malabar (Kerala). Features: lagoons called kayals or backwaters (Vembanad Lake), estuaries not deltas, many natural ports (Kandla, Mumbai, Marmagao, Kochi). A submergent coast.
Eastern coastal plain

Wider (up to 100 km or more), between the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal. Utkal plain (Odisha), Northern Circars (Andhra, between Mahanadi and Krishna), Coromandel coast (Krishna to Kanyakumari). Large deltas . The coast is emergent, so ports are fewer, and cyclone-prone. Chilika lake in Odisha is the largest coastal lagoon in India, and Pulicat is in Andhra and Tamil Nadu.
Emergent vs submergent coasts

An emergent coast is raised or has a falling sea level, giving smooth, straight shorelines, lagoons, sand bars and shallow water. A submergent coast is drowned, with a ragged shoreline and deep natural harbours. India's west is submergent, its east emergent. Remember this pairing for port questions.
Islands of the Arabian Sea

Lakshadweep : 36 islands, coral atolls, about 32 sq km, capital Kavaratti. The Eight Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the Maldives, and the Nine Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the rest of Lakshadweep. Others in the west: Diu, Elephanta, Salsette (Mumbai).
Islands of the Bay of Bengal

Andaman and Nicobar : about 572 islands, a submerged mountain chain, volcanic Barren Island is India's only active volcano. The Ten Degree Channel separates the Andamans from the Nicobars. Indira Point (Great Nicobar) is the southernmost tip of India. Saddle Peak (737 m) is the highest point. Other: Sriharikota, Pamban, Majuli (river island).
Great Nicobar and sensitive islands

The Great Nicobar Island project (about Rs 72,000 crore, including a transhipment port, airport and township) clashes with a biosphere reserve and tribal land of the Shompen. Supporters cite strategy near the Malacca Strait. Critics cite forest loss and the earthquake and tsunami risk.
Coasts and livelihoods

India has about 7,500 km of coastline, including islands (about 6,100 km on the mainland). Nine coastal states and four union territories. Coasts hold major ports, fisheries, salt pans and mangroves. Coastal erosion and sea-level rise threaten them, which is why the CRZ rules matter.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Compare the western and eastern coastal plains', 'Why are there more ports on the west coast?', 'Importance of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands'. List sub-regions from north to south with one feature each. Draw emergent vs submergent shorelines. For islands: strategic, ecological and tribal angles.
The Indian Monsoon
Monsoon is India's real finance minister

Monsoon gives about 75% of annual rainfall, and farming employs a big share of workers. A weak monsoon raises food prices and cuts rural income. It features in GS I (climate), GS III (agriculture) and even Essay papers.
What is the monsoon?

The word comes from the Arabic mausim , meaning season. It is a seasonal reversal of winds: south-west in summer, north-east in winter. India's monsoon is the strongest because of the big landmass of Asia, the Tibetan plateau and the Indian Ocean.
Classical and modern explanations

Classical (Halley, 1686) : land heats faster than sea, giving a bigger sea breeze. Modern theory (Flohn, 1950s) ties it to the shift of the ITCZ: when the Sun moves north, the trough moves over the Ganga plain, and the south-east trades cross the equator, turning right to become south-west monsoon.
The onset and the two branches
The Arabian Sea branch is stronger and hits the Western Ghats first. The Bay of Bengal branch brings rain to the north-east and the Ganga plains. Onset is sudden: the burst .
Dates of the monsoon

Dates are normal values set by IMD; the onset over Kerala has varied from late May to early June in recent years. Withdrawal takes about a month, and October heat is the retreating monsoon with clear skies.
Spatial pattern

India's average rainfall is about 117 cm. Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in Meghalaya get over 1,100 cm; Jaisalmer gets under 10 cm. The Rain shadow east of the Western Ghats gets little. The north-east monsoon (October to December) is the main rain for Tamil Nadu. Rain comes in spells . Break monsoon is a gap of days when the trough shifts to the Himalaya foothills.
What disturbs it

El Nino (usually weakens), IOD (positive helps), Eurasian snow , MJO (a 30-60 day pulse) and western disturbances are key. IMD gives Long Period Average forecasts: normal is 96 to 104% of LPA (87 cm for 1971-2020 base). 2023: about 94% of LPA (El Nino); 2024: about 108%, above normal.
Is the monsoon changing?

Studies suggest fewer rainy days but more extreme downpours: floods in Kerala (2018), Chennai (2015), Himachal (2023). Some see a long-term weakening from aerosols; others see recovery with warming. For answers, say that the mean may be steady but variability is rising, which hits dryland farmers hardest.
Monsoon and the economy

A good monsoon lifts kharif crops (rice, pulses, cotton), reservoirs, hydropower and rural demand. A bad one raises food inflation, leading to export curbs on rice or sugar (as in 2023). IMD issues forecasts in April and updates in May and June. Mission Mausam aims at better models. Crop insurance (PMFBY) and contingency plans cushion shocks.
How to write this

Likely questions "Explain the mechanism of the south-west monsoon. Why is its onset sudden?" (15 marks) "What are the causes of break in the monsoon?" (10 marks) Structure: mechanism (ITCZ, jets, Tibet) with a diagram; onset and withdrawal dates; regional pattern; risks; economy. Prelims tip: know the normal onset date, the tropical easterly jet, the 87 cm LPA, and the retreating monsoon in October.
Soils, Forests and Natural Vegetation of India
Soil and forest are slow capital

Soil takes centuries to form; forests take decades. They support farms, water and wildlife, and are central to India's climate promise. Expect UPSC to link them to land degradation , mangroves and forest law.
Eight Indian soil types
ICAR groups India's soils into eight: alluvial, black, red, laterite, arid, saline, peaty and forest soils. Alluvial soil is the largest and most fertile, with Khadar new and Bhangar old.
Black and red soils

Black soil (regur) forms from Deccan basalt. It is rich in clay, holds moisture, cracks in summer (so it "self-ploughs") and is high in lime, iron and magnesium, low in nitrogen and humus. It is the home of cotton. Red soil gets its colour from iron in crystalline rock. It is porous and poor in humus, nitrogen and lime. It turns yellow when hydrated. It occurs in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
Other soils

Laterite : leached by heavy rain; needs manure; suits tree crops. Arid : sandy, salty, low organic matter; Rajasthan. Saline and alkaline (reh, kallar, usar): too much salt, from poor irrigation. Peaty : Kerala (kari), rich in organic matter. Forest : hill soils, acidic in higher areas.
Soil erosion and conservation

Forms: sheet, rill and gully (the Chambal ravines). Causes: deforestation, over-grazing, heavy rain and bad ploughing. Remedies: contour ploughing , terracing , strip cropping, shelter belts , check dams and afforestation. The Central Soil Conservation Board was set up in 1953.
Forest types
Classification follows Champion and Seth (1968) : 16 major types. Rainfall is the main control, with temperature and altitude. Himalayan forests change with height in belts.
Forest cover today

As of ISFR 2023 , forest cover is about 21.76% of India's area; forest and tree cover together make about 25.2% (ISFR 2023). The target in the National Forest Policy 1988 is 33% of area (two thirds in hills). Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest cover in area; Mizoram the highest share. Very dense forest is only a small slice, so quality matters more than the headline.
Mangroves and tidal forests
Mangroves have stilt and breathing roots, protect coasts from storm surge and nurse fish. India has about 4,990 sq km (ISFR 2023); West Bengal leads.
Development versus forests

The Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023 exempts some categories (like linear projects near borders and security land) from clearance. Supporters see faster infrastructure; critics fear loss of undocumented forests. The Great Nicobar project raises a similar clash. Tribal rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 add a third view.
Policies and programmes

Green India Mission , CAMPA (compensatory afforestation funds), the Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam plantation drive (2024) and a pledge at COP26 for a 2.5-3 billion tonne carbon sink by 2030. Soil: Soil Health Card (2015) and Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana promote organic farming.
How to write this

Likely questions "Why is black soil considered the best for cotton? Where is it found?" (10 marks) "Discuss the status of mangroves in India and why they matter." (10 marks) Structure: classify; give origin of each soil with a crop; forest types by rainfall; recent data; law and policy. Prelims tip: memorise ISFR headline numbers, the biggest mangrove area (Sundarbans), and who proposed forest types (Champion and Seth).
Water Resources and River Interlinking
India has 18% of people and 4% of water

Water is the sharpest long-term constraint on India's growth. Rainfall is seasonal, rivers are unevenly spread, and groundwater is falling. UPSC links this to agriculture , federalism (water is a state subject) and interlinking .
How much water is there?

BCM means billion cubic metres. Only a fraction can be stored or used. India's per capita availability has fallen from about 5,000 cubic m in 1951 to about 1,500 in 2021, so India is officially water-stressed .
Where it goes

Irrigation dominates use. Groundwater supplies about 60% of irrigation and 85% of rural drinking water. India is the world's largest extractor of groundwater, which is why states like Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan have many over-exploited blocks.
Dams and multipurpose projects

Big dams: Bhakra (Sutlej), Hirakud (Mahanadi), Tehri (Bhagirathi, tallest in India), Sardar Sarovar (Narmada). Dams give irrigation, power, flood control and water supply, but cause displacement, siltation and loss of habitat. Jawaharlal Nehru called dams the temples of modern India.
Interlinking: the idea

Surplus river basins (Brahmaputra, Ganga, Mahanadi) could pass water to deficit ones (Cauvery, Pennar, western Rajasthan). The National Perspective Plan (1980) proposed 30 links: 16 peninsular and 14 Himalayan. The NWDA (1982) studies them. The Supreme Court in 2012 directed the Centre to act.
The Ken-Betwa link

The first project under the national plan was approved in 2021 and its foundation stone laid in December 2024. It moves water from the Ken to the Betwa for drought-hit Bundelkhand across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. It will submerge part of the Panna Tiger Reserve, a main criticism.
Is interlinking wise?

For: drought and flood relief, irrigation, navigation. Against: huge cost, displacement, damaged ecosystems, effects on the Ganga delta and monsoon, and state disputes over whether any state has a "surplus". Critics favour cheaper local options: rainwater harvesting , watershed work, drip irrigation, and fixing leaky canals.
Interstate disputes and law

Water is a State subject (Entry 17, State List), but Article 262 lets Parliament settle interstate river disputes through the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 . Tribunals have sat for Cauvery (award 2007, modified by the Supreme Court in 2018), Krishna and Godavari. Disputes drag on for decades.
Programmes

Jal Shakti Ministry (2019); Jal Jeevan Mission (2019): tap water to every rural home; Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019): community groundwater management in stressed areas; PMKSY (2015): "more crop per drop"; Amrit Sarovar (2022): 75 ponds per district; and the Jal Shakti Abhiyan catch-the-rain campaign.
How to write this

Likely questions "Examine the feasibility of river interlinking in India." (15 marks) "How can India address groundwater depletion?" (10 marks) Structure: status; opportunity; concerns (ecology, federal, costs); alternatives; give Ken-Betwa as a current test. Prelims tip: NWDA, the 30 links, Article 262, and the Ken-Betwa states are repeat hits.
Western Disturbances, Winter and Retreating Monsoon
India has four seasons, not just a monsoon

IMD recognises four seasons: cold weather (December to February), hot weather (March to May), southwest monsoon (June to September) and retreating monsoon or post-monsoon (October to November). The winter and retreat phases matter for rabi crops, cyclones and cold waves.
Winter circulation

In winter a cold, dry high-pressure area forms over northwest India and Central Asia. Dry winds blow out from the land as the northeast trades . Temperatures fall from south to north: about 24-25 degrees C on the Tamil Nadu coast, 10-15 degrees C in the plains of the north. The jet stream sits south of the Himalaya at about 25-30 degrees N and shapes weather.
Western disturbances

Western disturbances are low-pressure systems born over the Mediterranean region, travelling east on the subtropical westerly jet through Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan. They bring winter rain to Punjab, Haryana and Delhi, and snow to the western Himalaya. Their rain is vital for rabi wheat , locally called mahawat in the north. They are most frequent from December to February, usually 4-6 a month.
Why they matter

Benefits: wheat, barley, mustard and horticulture (apple in Himachal and Kashmir) depend on them, and snow feeds rivers. Risks: heavy rain with hail can flatten crops; snowfall causes avalanches; when they are strong or interact with the monsoon, they can cause floods, as in Uttarakhand 2013 and Kashmir 2014. Fog and cold wave in the Indo-Gangetic plain arise when disturbances are weak and skies clear.
Cold wave, fog and local winters

A cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature falls to 4 degrees C or less (plains) or a departure of 4.5 degrees C or more from normal. Dense winter fog hits Delhi and the plains. Rainfall in winter also comes to Tamil Nadu coast from the northeast monsoon from October to December.
Retreating monsoon (October to November)

The monsoon withdraws from northwest India in September and from the rest by mid-October. Skies clear, but humidity stays high. The temperature rises, giving the October heat , a muggy spell. Low-pressure systems move from the Andaman Sea to the east coast and the Bay of Bengal becomes cyclone-prone: most severe cyclones in the Bay hit in October-November.
Northeast monsoon

As the trough shifts south, winds blow from the northeast over the Bay of Bengal, pick up moisture and bring rain to the Tamil Nadu coast, Puducherry and south Andhra. This gives Tamil Nadu most of its annual rain. It supports the second crop of rice (samba). In the Chennai floods of 2015, this season's rains were the cause.
Are western disturbances changing?

Studies suggest that warming of the Arctic and shifts in the jet stream may be changing their number and strength. Some research links fewer winter disturbances to dry winters, and more intense ones to extreme rain events. The evidence is still being worked out, so examiners expect balanced answers.
Winter crops and agencies

The rabi sowing season of October to December depends on this phase. IMD issues cold wave and fog alerts. The Himalayan snow from these systems helps feed the Indus and Ganga, and shifting patterns affect water security. The Kashmir valley's Chillai Kalan , the harshest 40 days from 21 December, is a local cold spell.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'What are western disturbances and why are they important?', 'Explain the northeast monsoon', 'Why do east coast cyclones peak in October-November?' Define, give origin, path, season and effect, in that order. Mention rabi wheat and horticulture. Link retreating monsoon to cyclone season and the Tamil Nadu rainfall.
Himalayan Rivers: Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra
Three river systems, three personalities

The Himalayan rivers are perennial, fed by rain and snow. They carry huge silt, form big plains and deltas, and cross borders. UPSC asks about tributaries, courses, hydro projects, floods and treaties. Learn each river's source, major tributaries, and what is special about it.
Drainage basics

A drainage system is a river and its tributaries. A catchment is the area drained. A watershed separates basins. Himalayan rivers show antecedent drainage : they existed before the Himalaya rose and cut deep gorges through them as the mountains rose. They erode headward and have much river capture .
Indus system

Source near Mansarovar in Tibet. Flows through Ladakh, Gilgit and Pakistan to the Arabian Sea, about 2,900 km (about 1,114 km in India). Tributaries: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Satluj (the five rivers of Punjab). The Indus Waters Treaty (1960, World Bank mediated) gave India the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Satluj) and Pakistan the western (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab), with limited use for India. India placed the treaty in abeyance in April 2025.
Ganga system

The Bhagirathi rises at Gaumukh (Gangotri). At Devprayag it joins the Alaknanda , and the river becomes the Ganga. Total length about 2,525 km. It enters the plains at Haridwar. Left bank tributaries: Ramganga, Gomti, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi, Mahananda . Right bank: Yamuna, Son , Chambal (via Yamuna), Betwa, Ken. In Bangladesh it is called the Padma, joins the Brahmaputra and ends in the Bay of Bengal.
Prayags and the Alaknanda

Five prayags (confluences) on the Alaknanda: Vishnuprayag (with the Dhauliganga), Nandprayag (Nandakini), Karnaprayag (Pindar), Rudraprayag (Mandakini), Devprayag (with the Bhagirathi). Allahabad (Prayagraj) is where the Ganga meets the Yamuna. The Ganga was declared the national river in 2008. The Namami Gange programme started in 2014 for cleaning it.
Yamuna, Ghaghara, Kosi

The Yamuna rises at Yamunotri, the largest tributary by length. The Ghaghara carries the most water among Ganga's tributaries. The Kosi is the 'Sorrow of Bihar' for shifting course. The Son is the large right-bank tributary from the plateau. The Damodar is the 'Sorrow of Bengal' and flows to the Hooghly.
Brahmaputra

Rises near Mansarovar as the Tsangpo in Tibet. Flows east, turns at the Namcha Barwa and enters Arunachal as the Dihang (Siang) . Meets the Dibang and Lohit to become the Brahmaputra in Assam. Enters Bangladesh as the Jamuna . It is braided, floods in monsoon, and has the river island Majuli . Major left bank tributaries: Dibang, Lohit, Dhansiri. Right bank: Subansiri, Kameng, Manas, Sankosh, Teesta.
Water sharing and dams

China is building a very large hydropower scheme on the Yarlung Tsangpo near the Great Bend, announced in 2024-25. India plans the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project as a counter-buffer, which faces local protest. India and Bangladesh signed the Ganga Water Treaty in 1996 (30 years) and have not signed the Teesta deal. These make river issues strategic.
Basins by size

Ganga basin is the largest in India (about 26 percent of the country's area), followed by the Indus and Godavari. Brahmaputra carries the highest water volume among Indian rivers. The Ganga plains are the most densely populated river basin in the world, which makes pollution and groundwater stress central issues.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Himalayan vs peninsular rivers', 'The Indus Waters Treaty', 'Why does the Brahmaputra flood Assam?', 'Namami Gange'. Draw a schematic of the Ganga with left and right tributaries. For floods: monsoon rain, snowmelt, silt and braiding, earthquakes, landslide dams. Always add a policy hook: treaties, NMCG, flood forecasting.
Peninsular Rivers: Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery and Narmada
Rain-fed rivers with water disputes

Peninsular rivers are seasonal, fed mainly by monsoon rain. They have fixed courses because of hard rock, no deep valleys and no meanders. They cause a string of inter-state disputes. UPSC asks about their courses, tributaries, delta, rift valley and disputes.
How they differ from Himalayan rivers

Seasonal, not perennial (no glacier). Shorter, shallow valleys, nearly graded. Little erosion; they form deltas in the east and estuaries in the west. Flow mainly east (Bay of Bengal), because the plateau slopes east. Older: they have reached maturity.
Godavari

The longest peninsular river (about 1,465 km), the 'Dakshin Ganga'. Rises at Trimbak near Nashik. Tributaries: Pranhita (carries the Wardha and Wainganga), Indravati, Manjira, Sabari. Drains into the Bay of Bengal in a big delta in Andhra Pradesh. Basin states: Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra, Chhattisgarh, Odisha. Polavaram project is on it.
Krishna

Second longest peninsular river (about 1,400 km). Rises at Mahabaleshwar in the Western Ghats. Tributaries: Koyna, Panchganga, Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, Bhima, Tungabhadra, Musi. Ends in a delta in Andhra. Srisailam and Nagarjuna Sagar dams. Disputes among Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra.
Cauvery

Rises at Talakaveri in Brahmagiri hills, Karnataka. Tributaries: Hemavati, Lokapavani, Shimsha, Arkavathi, Kabini, Bhavani, Amravati. Flows in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, forming Shivanasamudram falls and a delta near Kaveripattinam. The Cauvery gets rain in both the southwest monsoon (upper) and the northeast monsoon (lower), so it flows nearly all year.
Narmada and Tapi

The Narmada rises at Amarkantak (Madhya Pradesh), flows west in a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura, and forms the Dhuandhar falls near Jabalpur, then enters the Gulf of Khambhat in an estuary. About 1,312 km. Sardar Sarovar Dam. The Tapi rises at Multai (Betul), flows west and ends in the Gulf of Khambhat at Surat. Both flow west and make estuaries, not deltas.
Other east and west flowing rivers

East: Mahanadi (Chhattisgarh to Odisha, Hirakud dam), Subarnarekha , Brahmani , Penner , Vaigai . West: Sabarmati , Mahi , Luni (inland), Sharavati (Jog falls), Periyar (longest in Kerala), Bharathapuzha . Western Ghats rivers are short and fast and meet the sea in estuaries.
River water disputes

Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1990, award 2007; the Supreme Court modified it in 2018). Krishna (Bachawat Tribunal 1969; Brijesh Kumar Tribunal 2010, award 2013). Godavari (Tribunal 1969). Mahadayi (tribunal award 2018, dispute with Goa and Karnataka). Article 262 empowers Parliament to set up tribunals, and the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 is the law.
Rivers and development

Peninsular rivers feed delta rice bowls in Godavari-Krishna and Thanjavur, and hydropower. Seasonality means storage dams are vital. The linking idea (Ken-Betwa, Godavari-Cauvery) aims to move surplus water. The National Water Policy treats water as a state subject under the Constitution (Entry 17, State List), with Union role for inter-state rivers (Entry 56, Union List).
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Why do Narmada and Tapi form estuaries?', 'Distinguish Himalayan and peninsular drainage', 'Cauvery dispute'. Always a two-column comparison on origin, flow, valley, delta, use. Give the rift valley explanation. For disputes, state law, tribunal, key SC order and the way forward.
Alluvial, Black, Red and Laterite Soils
Soil decides what grows where

The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) grouped Indian soils into eight major groups. UPSC asks for formation, distribution, characteristics and crops. Master the big four: alluvial, black, red and laterite. Then add arid, forest, saline and peaty.
How soils form

Soil comes from parent rock , climate , relief , organisms and time (Dokuchaev's factors). Hot, wet climates leach nutrients. Dry climates leave salts. Soil profile layers are called horizons: O, A, B, C, R.
Alluvial soil

The largest group (about 40 percent of the land). Found in the northern plains, the coastal plains and deltas. Deposited by rivers, loose and fertile. Rich in potash and lime, poor in nitrogen and humus. Types: Bhangar and Khadar . Crops: wheat, rice, sugarcane, jute, pulses. Highly productive, so it supports dense population.
Black (regur) soil

Formed from Deccan basalt . Found in Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Andhra. Clayey, retains moisture, swells when wet and cracks when dry , which gives it a self-ploughing quality. Rich in iron, lime, calcium, magnesium; poor in nitrogen and phosphorus. Black colour from titaniferous magnetite. Best for cotton , hence 'black cotton soil'; also sugarcane, soybean, millets.
Red and yellow soil

Forms on ancient crystalline rocks (granite, gneiss) in areas of low rain: Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Northeast. Red colour from iron oxide in the anhydrous state; yellow when hydrated. Porous, low in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus. Need fertiliser and irrigation. Crops: groundnut, millets, pulses, tobacco.
Laterite soil

Latin later means brick. Forms in heavy rain with alternate wet and dry seasons. Intense leaching removes silica and leaves iron and aluminium. Found in the Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, Meghalaya, Odisha, Karnataka and Kerala. Acidic, poor in nutrients and humus. Hardens into brick when dry, so it is used for building. Supports tea, coffee, rubber, cashew, tapioca.
Other soils

Arid (desert) : sandy, saline, low humus, western Rajasthan. Needs irrigation (Indira Gandhi Canal). Forest (mountain) : Himalayan slopes, humus rich, acidic in snow areas. Saline and alkaline : reh, kallar, usar, in Punjab, Haryana, UP, Gujarat; from over-irrigation. Reclaim with gypsum. Peaty and marshy : Kerala (kari soil), Sundarbans, rich in organic matter.
Soil degradation

Problems: erosion (sheet, rill, gully), salinity, waterlogging, loss of organic carbon, fertiliser overuse. About 30 percent of land is degraded by some estimates, and India has committed to restore 26 million hectares by 2030 under UNCCD. Counter measures: Soil Health Card (2015), contour bunding, shelterbelts, zero tillage, afforestation.
Soil and crop pairs

Alluvial: wheat and rice. Black: cotton. Red: groundnut and millets. Laterite: plantation crops. Arid: bajra with irrigation. The Soil Health Card scheme, launched in 2015, tests soil every two years and advises balanced fertiliser use. ICAR's National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (Nagpur) does mapping.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Why is black soil suited to cotton?', 'Account for laterite soil in the Western Ghats', 'Soil erosion and conservation'. Use cause (rock, climate), property, distribution, crop in that order. Draw a rough map with four colours. For degradation, mention erosion, salinity and the Soil Health Card.
Mangroves, Wetlands and Biosphere Reserves of India
Protected landscapes appear every year

Biosphere reserves, wetlands and mangroves are standard prelims facts and mains themes about conservation. Each sits in a legal and international framework. Know the numbers, the largest examples and the way each is protected.
Mangroves

Salt-tolerant forests of tidal coasts. Features: pneumatophores (breathing roots), prop roots, viviparous seeds, salt glands. They stabilise shores, buffer cyclones and tsunamis, and store blue carbon . India's mangrove area is about 4,992 sq km (ISFR 2021), about 0.15 percent of the land. West Bengal (Sundarbans) has the largest cover, then Gujarat, then Andaman and Nicobar.
Mangrove types and threats

Common species: Rhizophora, Avicennia, Sonneratia, and Heritiera fomes (sundari) in the Sundarbans. Other sites: Bhitarkanika (Odisha), Godavari-Krishna delta, Pichavaram (Tamil Nadu). Threats: aquaculture ponds, reclamation, sand mining and oil pollution. Protected by the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ-I). The MISHTI scheme (2023) promotes planting.
Wetlands and Ramsar

A wetland holds water over land, for part or all of the year. The Ramsar Convention (Iran, 1971) lists wetlands of international importance. India joined in 1982. As of 2024 India had over 80 Ramsar sites, among the highest in Asia (check the latest count). Examples: Chilika (first, 1981), Keoladeo, Loktak, Sundarbans, Wular, Sambhar, Ashtamudi, Vembanad, Harike.
Montreux Record and rules

The Montreux Record lists Ramsar sites facing damage. In India, Loktak is on it; Chilika was listed and then removed in 2002. The Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 replaced the 2010 rules and shifted powers to states. The National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems (NPCA) funds work.
Biosphere reserves

A biosphere reserve (BR) follows UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere programme (1971). It has three zones: core (strict protection), buffer (limited research and eco-friendly use) and transition (people live and work). India has 18 BRs, of which 12 are in the UNESCO network. India's first: Nilgiri (1986). Other BRs: Nanda Devi, Nokrek, Manas, Sundarbans, Gulf of Mannar, Great Nicobar, Simlipal, Dibru-Saikhowa, Dehang-Debang, Pachmarhi, Achanakmar-Amarkantak, Kachchh, Cold Desert, Seshachalam, Panna, Agasthyamala, Khangchendzonga.
Reserve names and states

Nilgiri: Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka. Agasthyamala: Kerala, Tamil Nadu. Sundarbans: West Bengal. Gulf of Mannar: Tamil Nadu (marine). Cold Desert: Himachal Pradesh (Spiti). Nokrek: Meghalaya. Simlipal: Odisha. Pachmarhi: Madhya Pradesh. Kachchh: Gujarat, the largest by area.
People and protection

Core areas often displace forest dwellers. The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises rights, but conflict persists over critical wildlife habitats. Advocates of 'fortress conservation' say people harm wildlife, while advocates of community conservation point to sacred groves and community reserves that work well.
Related categories

National parks (stricter), wildlife sanctuaries, conservation reserves, community reserves, all under the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972. Biosphere reserves are not a legal category under this Act; they are an administrative designation. Ramsar sites also need no separate legal status, though many sit inside parks.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Role of mangroves in coastal protection', 'What are biosphere reserves and how do they differ from national parks?', 'Ramsar sites in India'. Distinguish zones and use. Give three examples each with states. Link to blue carbon, cyclone buffers and livelihoods.
Agriculture: Cropping Patterns and Irrigation
Farming employs nearly half of India

Agriculture and allied sectors employ about 46% of workers but give about 18% of GVA (as of recent years). So farm policy is a big political economy issue. UPSC mixes geography (where, why) with policy (MSP, irrigation, diversification).
Farming types and seasons
Types: subsistence , commercial , plantation (tea, coffee, rubber), shifting (jhum in the Northeast), dry farming in under 75 cm rain regions, and intensive farming in the plains.
Main crops and where they grow

Crops follow rainfall, temperature and soil. Rice is the staple of the east and south. Wheat dominates the north-west. Millets (shree anna) grow in dry regions; 2023 was the International Year of Millets.
Cash and plantation crops

Cotton and jute are fibres; jute grows in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta of West Bengal. Sugarcane is needed for sugar mills. Tea (Assam), coffee (Karnataka, Kodagu) and rubber (Kerala) are plantations. India is the second largest producer of tea and of rice, wheat and sugar too, as of recent data.
Irrigation

Net irrigated area is about 55% of net sown area. Wells and tubewells lead because they are cheap and farmer-controlled, but they deplete the groundwater table. Tanks are common where rock is hard. Drip and sprinkler systems save water.
The Green Revolution

From the mid-1960s, HYV seeds (Norman Borlaug; M.S. Swaminathan in India), fertiliser, irrigation and credit raised wheat and then rice output in Punjab, Haryana and western UP. India became self-sufficient in food grains. Limits: regional and crop bias, soil degradation, falling water tables.
Is the Punjab model sustainable?

Punjab and Haryana grow rice in a dry region because MSP and procurement favour it. Groundwater falls about a metre a year in some blocks, and stubble burning pollutes Delhi. Experts urge crop diversification to pulses, maize and oilseeds, direct-seeded rice and price signals. Others warn farmers will not shift without assured purchase.
Policy at a glance

MSP is declared by the Centre on CACP advice for 22 crops plus FRP for sugarcane. PM-KISAN (2019) gives cash. PMFBY (2016) is crop insurance. e-NAM links mandis. The three farm laws were repealed in 2021 after farmer protests. The government's target is to double farmer income, widely seen as missed.
New frontiers

Horticulture output now exceeds food grains. Operation Flood (1970) made India the largest milk producer. The Northeast and Odisha show jhum being replaced slowly. Natural farming mission launched in 2024 and drone use (Namo Drone Didi) are fresh themes. The Kharif crops depend on monsoon; Rabi on stored moisture and irrigation.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the changing cropping pattern in India and its causes." (10 marks) "Examine the importance of irrigation in Indian agriculture." (10 marks) Structure: trend in numbers; physical factors; policy factors (MSP, irrigation); impact (water, soil); way forward. Prelims tip: match crops to seasons and states; rice is kharif; wheat is rabi; MSP is set on CACP advice.
Minerals and Energy Resources
Minerals build, energy drives

India's rise needs steel, aluminium, power and fuel. The geography question is where the resources are and why industry sits near them. The new question is critical minerals and the move to clean energy.
Mineral belts of India

Most metallic minerals lie in the old rocks of the peninsula . The Himalayan region has few. The Gangetic plains have almost none, apart from building materials. Mining is regulated by the MMDR Act, 1957 , amended in 2015, 2021 and 2023.
Key minerals at a glance

Iron ore types: hematite (best, about 60-70% iron) and magnetite (highest iron content). Famous mines: Bailadila (Chhattisgarh), Kudremukh (Karnataka), Noamundi (Jharkhand). India has large reserves of iron ore, mica and bauxite but is short of coking coal and copper.
Coal

Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Odisha hold the biggest reserves. Jharia is the main coking coal field; Raniganj (West Bengal) is the oldest. India produced over one billion tonnes of coal in 2024-25 (as of 2025), yet still imports coking coal.
Petroleum and gas

First oil: Digboi in Assam (1889). Main fields: Mumbai High (offshore), Assam, Gujarat (Ankleshwar, Cambay) and the Krishna-Godavari basin. India imports about 85% of its crude oil (as of recent data). Strategic reserves are at Vishakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.
Power sources
Hydro projects: Bhakra, Tehri, Koyna. Nuclear: India uses uranium and plans a three-stage programme to use its large thorium reserves in Kerala sands. Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu has Russian reactors.
Renewables and green hydrogen

The Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan is among the world's largest. Wind is big in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat. India's target: 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070 . The International Solar Alliance (2015) is headquartered in Gurugram. The National Green Hydrogen Mission began in 2023. Non-fossil sources reached about half of installed capacity in 2025.
Coal now, clean later?

Coal supplies most of India's electricity and mines support lakhs of jobs in Jharkhand and Odisha. A fast shutdown would hurt them. But coal causes air pollution and emissions. The debate centres on a just transition : retrain workers, keep coal for baseload, and add storage plus renewables, while demand grows.
Critical minerals

Lithium, cobalt and rare earths are needed for batteries and magnets. India found lithium at Reasi in J&K (2023) and set up the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025). Overseas, KABIL buys assets in Argentina and Australia. China's control of processing worries India.
How to write this

Likely questions "Describe the distribution of iron ore in India and its role in steel plant location." (10 marks) "Is India's energy transition feasible without coal?" (15 marks) Structure: distribution; link to industries; problems (imports, environment); energy mix; policy such as the 2030 and 2070 goals. Prelims tip: Gondwana coal is 98%; Digboi is the first oil field; Jharia is the coking coal hub.
Industrial Location and Industrial Regions
Where factories go

Factories choose places to cut cost and raise sales. The answer shapes cities, rivers, ports and regional inequality. For UPSC, you must explain why an industry is located where it is , and link it to current manufacturing policy.
Weber's location theory

Alfred Weber (1909) argued firms pick the point with the least transport cost , then adjust for labour and agglomeration. If the raw material loses weight in processing (ore to iron), the factory goes near the raw material. If it gains weight or is perishable, it goes to the market.
Factors of location in India

Raw material, power, water, labour, capital, market, transport, government policy and history all matter. Weight-losing industries such as iron and steel and sugar go near sources. Footloose industries such as IT and electronics can go anywhere, so skilled labour and urban facilities decide.
Iron and steel

Steel plants sit in the Chotanagpur belt because iron ore, coking coal, limestone and manganese are close. After 1990 the private sector and coastal sites (Visakhapatnam, Gujarat Hazira) rose. India is the second largest crude steel producer, after China (as of recent data).
Cotton, sugar and other industries

Cotton textiles : early mills in Mumbai (1854) and Ahmedabad thanks to port, capital and cotton; now spread widely, with spinning in the south. Sugar : shifted from UP to Maharashtra because cane has higher sucrose in the tropical climate and cooperatives helped. Cement : near limestone. Aluminium : near cheap power and bauxite.
Industrial regions
Other regions: Chotanagpur , Delhi-Gurugram-Meerut, and Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram. Most clusters grew around ports and old mineral belts. Eastern India has resources but lags in new industry.
Policy and corridors

Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 gave the public sector a dominant role; 1991 liberalised licensing. Make in India (2014) and PLI schemes (2020) aim to lift manufacturing to 25% of GDP. Industrial corridors (Delhi-Mumbai, Chennai-Bengaluru) and SEZs (Act 2005) cluster factories. PM GatiShakti (2021) coordinates transport links.
Spread industry or let clusters grow?

Clusters bring economies of scale, but regional inequality grows: four states (Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Karnataka) host a large share of factory output. Policy tools like tax holidays and corridors in backward areas are used. Critics point to land acquisition, displacement and pollution in such sites.
Current moves

Semiconductor fabs in Dholera (Gujarat) and Assam, mobile phone assembly in Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh, and defence corridors in UP and Tamil Nadu are the newest clusters. Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra lead in electronics and autos. MSMEs account for about a third of manufacturing output.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the factors influencing the location of iron and steel industry in India." (10 marks) "Account for the decline of Mumbai textile mills and the rise of Surat." (10 marks) Structure: theory first (Weber), then Indian factors, examples, regional pattern, policy. Prelims tip: TISCO is the oldest steel plant; Bhilai and Bokaro came with the USSR; Rourkela with Germany; Durgapur with the UK.
Transport and Communication
Roads and ports make markets

Transport links farms to cities and India to the world. High logistics costs cut competitiveness. In GS I you must explain patterns of networks ; in GS III you link them to growth and trade, so both views are needed.
Modes at a glance
India has the second largest road network in the world, over 60 lakh km, of which national highways are about 1.4 lakh km. Roads carry the largest share, which raises costs and emissions.
Roads and expressways

The National Highways Authority of India was set up in 1988. Projects: the Golden Quadrilateral, the North-South and East-West corridors (7,300 km) and Bharatmala (2017). Expressways such as Delhi-Mumbai are underway. PMGSY (2000) connects villages.
Railways

The first train ran from Bombay to Thane in 1853 (34 km). Indian Railways is run by the state and divided into 17 zones. The network is among the world's largest by route length (about 68,000 km). Dedicated Freight Corridors (Eastern: Ludhiana to Sonnagar; Western: Dadri to JNPT) free up passenger lines. Vande Bharat trains and the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project are the newest steps.
Ports and shipping

Around 95% of trade by volume and about 70% by value moves by sea. Sagarmala (2015) aims at port-led growth. A new deep-water Vadhavan port in Maharashtra was approved in 2024, and Vizhinjam in Kerala is the first deep-water transhipment port (opened in 2025).
Waterways and air

NW-1 on the Ganga (Haldia to Prayagraj, 1,620 km), NW-2 on the Brahmaputra (Dhubri to Sadiya) and NW-3 on the West Coast canal are the first three. The 2016 Act declared 111 national waterways. Airways: UDAN (2016) links small cities; the airport count more than doubled in a decade (as of 2024).
Communication

India has the second largest telecom subscriber base. 5G launched in October 2022. Digital India (2015), BharatNet for villages, and UPI now account for the largest volume of real-time payments in the world. Postal network is the largest by number of outlets. ISRO satellites (INSAT, GSAT) support all of this.
Roads, rail or water?

Logistics cost in India is about 8% of GDP by the official NCAER estimate (2024), down from older estimates of 13-14% (figures vary by method). Experts urge a shift from roads to rail and waterways. The National Logistics Policy (2022) and PM GatiShakti seek this. Critics say inland waterways have too little traffic to justify costs.
Connectivity and geopolitics

Chabahar port (Iran) offers a route to Afghanistan and Central Asia, avoiding Pakistan. The International North-South Transport Corridor links India, Iran and Russia. The India-Middle East-Europe Corridor ( IMEC , announced at G20, 2023) is another plan. Border roads and tunnels in the Himalaya (Atal Tunnel, 2020) serve security as well as trade.
How to write this

Likely questions "Examine the role of inland waterways in India's transport system." (10 marks) "How do ports and logistics determine export competitiveness?" (15 marks) Structure: mode share; problems; schemes; modal shift; link to geopolitics. Prelims tip: NW-1 is on the Ganga; GQ links the four metros; Sagarmala is for ports; UDAN is for regional air connectivity.
Green Revolution, Major Crops and Agro-climatic Zones
From ship-to-mouth to food surplus

India imported wheat under PL-480 in the early 1960s. The Green Revolution turned it into a grain-surplus country. UPSC asks about its causes, effects, regional imbalance and the next steps, plus crop seasons and zones.
Crop seasons

Kharif : sown June-July with the monsoon, harvested September-October. Rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, jute, groundnut, soybean. Rabi : sown October-December, harvested April-June. Wheat, barley, gram, peas, mustard, linseed. Zaid : short summer season, March-June: watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, fodder.
The Green Revolution

Launched in 1966-67. Norman Borlaug developed dwarf wheat; M S Swaminathan led its adoption in India. Elements: high-yielding varieties (HYV: Sonalika, Kalyan Sona, IR-8 rice), irrigation, fertiliser and pesticide, minimum support price (MSP) and procurement through the Food Corporation of India (1965) and the Agricultural Prices Commission (now CACP). C Subramaniam was the Agriculture Minister.
Gains

Foodgrain output rose from about 82 million tonnes in 1960-61 to over 300 million tonnes in recent years. Wheat output jumped, mainly in Punjab, Haryana and western UP. India became self-sufficient in grain and now exports rice. Buffer stocks protect against drought, and the National Food Security Act (2013) uses them.
Costs and criticism

Regional imbalance : benefited northwest more than east and rainfed zones. Crop imbalance : wheat and rice over pulses and oilseeds. Environment : groundwater depletion, salinity, pesticide residue, soil nutrient loss. Inequality : large farmers gained more. The 'second Green Revolution' and 'evergreen revolution' (Swaminathan) stress sustainability, eastern India and pulses.
Other revolutions

White Revolution (Operation Flood, 1970, Verghese Kurien, NDDB). Blue Revolution (fisheries). Yellow Revolution (oilseeds). Pink (prawn, onion), Silver (eggs), Golden (horticulture). India is the world's largest milk producer.
Major crops and leading states

Rice : West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab. Wheat : Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Madhya Pradesh. Sugarcane : UP, Maharashtra, Karnataka. Cotton : Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana. Jute : West Bengal. Tea : Assam. Coffee : Karnataka. Rubber : Kerala. Rankings shift year to year; check the latest data before the exam.
Agro-climatic zones

The Planning Commission divided India into 15 agro-climatic zones (1989) for planning, using soil, rainfall and temperature. The National Agricultural Research Project of ICAR had 127 sub-zones. Examples: Western Himalayan, Eastern Himalayan, Lower Gangetic Plain, Middle Gangetic Plain, Upper Gangetic Plain, Trans-Gangetic Plain, Eastern Plateau and Hills, Central Plateau, Western Plateau, Southern Plateau, East Coast Plains, West Coast Plains, Gujarat Plains, Western Dry, Islands.
Today's challenges

MSP is legally available for 23 crops, but procurement is concentrated on wheat and rice. Schemes such as PM-KISAN (2019), PM Fasal Bima Yojana (2016) and the push for millets (International Year of Millets 2023) try to diversify. Punjab's paddy stubble burning and groundwater fall show Green Revolution costs.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Green Revolution: achievements and limitations', 'Why has it not reached eastern India?', 'Agro-climatic regional planning'. Balanced answer: gains, costs, the way forward. Mention HYV, irrigation, MSP, FCI. For the way forward: crop diversification, micro-irrigation, millets, eastern India focus.
Coal, Iron Ore and Bauxite Distribution
Minerals decide where industry grows

India's mineral map is concentrated: most coal and iron ore lie in the east of the peninsular plateau. This clustering explains the steel belt and the mining politics of Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh. UPSC asks for location, reasons and policy.
Types of coal

From oldest and best to youngest: anthracite (over 80 percent carbon, rare, in J&K), bituminous (the main coking coal), sub-bituminous and lignite (brown coal, low carbon). Peat is the earliest stage. India's coal is mostly bituminous and sub-bituminous, with high ash (30-45 percent) and low sulphur.
Coalfields

Gondwana coal (about 98 percent of reserves, 250 million years old): Damodar valley (Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro, Karanpura), Son valley, Mahanadi valley (Talcher, Ib), Godavari valley (Singareni). Tertiary coal in the northeast (Assam, Meghalaya): high sulphur. Lignite : Neyveli (Tamil Nadu), Gujarat, Rajasthan.
Leading coal states

Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh hold the largest reserves; Odisha and Chhattisgarh lead output in recent years. Jharia is the main coking coal field. India is the second largest coal producer and has crossed 1 billion tonnes of production (2023-24). Coal still gives about 70 percent of electricity.
Iron ore

Types: hematite (best, about 60-70 percent iron), magnetite (up to 72 percent; Karnataka, Kerala, Goa), limonite . The oldest rocks, the Dharwar and Iron Ore Series , hold them. Belts: Odisha-Jharkhand (Singhbhum, Keonjhar, Sundargarh, Bonai), Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur (Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra; Bailadila with the Kirandul), Bellary-Hospet (Karnataka), Kudremukh (Karnataka) and Goa, mostly exported from Marmagao.
Bauxite and aluminium

Bauxite is the ore of aluminium. Found in laterite caps: Odisha (Koraput, Kalahandi; Panchpatmali), Gujarat, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra. Aluminium smelters: Korba, Hirakud, Renukoot, Mettur, Alupuram. Smelting needs huge electricity, so plants sit near power. India is among the top producers of aluminium.
Other key minerals

Manganese (steel alloy): Odisha, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh. Copper : Khetri (Rajasthan), Malanjkhand (MP), Singhbhum. Mica : Jharkhand (Koderma), Andhra, Rajasthan. Limestone , gold (Kolar, Hutti in Karnataka). Uranium : Jaduguda (Jharkhand). Monazite and thorium: Kerala coast sands. Lithium : discovery in Reasi, J&K (2023).
Mining vs forests and tribes

Many mines lie in dense forest and Fifth Schedule tribal land. The Samatha judgment (1997) restricts transfer of tribal land. The Niyamgiri hill case (2013) upheld the gram sabha's right to refuse bauxite mining (Vedanta). The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act 1957 was amended in 2015 and 2021, and critical minerals were opened to auction. The 'resource curse' idea asks why mineral-rich districts remain poor.
Policy tools

District Mineral Foundation (2015) gives a share of royalty to affected people. The National Mineral Policy 2019 promotes exploration. Coal blocks were auctioned after the Supreme Court cancelled 214 allocations in 2014 (Manohar Lal Sharma case). The 2023 Critical Minerals List has 30 minerals, and the Critical Minerals Mission was approved in 2025.
How to answer

Likely questions: 'Why is the steel industry clustered in the east?', 'Distribution of coal', 'Coal mining and the environment'. Sketch a map with coal and iron belts and steel towns. Give the 98 percent Gondwana fact. Link to the district mineral fund and tribal rights.
Population, Migration and Urbanisation
People are the resource and the problem

India became the world's most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate). Numbers decide seats , grants , schemes and the economy. Age profile creates the demographic dividend . UPSC asks about trends, regional contrasts, migration and cities.
Key figures

Population growth has slowed. The fertility rate is now below the replacement level of 2.1. The census due in 2021 was delayed by COVID-19; the next census was announced for 2027 with caste enumeration (as of the 2025 notification).
Demographic transition

Stage 1 : high births, high deaths. Stage 2 : deaths fall first, population booms. Stage 3 : births fall. Stage 4 : low births, low deaths. Some add a fifth stage of ageing and decline (Japan). India's states are in different stages: Kerala and Tamil Nadu are late; Bihar and Uttar Pradesh are earlier.
Demographic dividend and ageing

A dividend arises when the working age (15-64) share is high. India's window runs to about 2040-50. It pays only if there are jobs, skills and health . Otherwise it is a "demographic burden". Southern states are ageing faster, with elderly share rising.
Migration

The 2011 Census counted about 45.6 crore migrants (37% of the population), mostly women moving for marriage. Men migrate for work. The 2020 lockdown exposed circular migrants' fragility; the One Nation One Ration Card and e-Shram portal followed.
Urbanisation

The urban share was 31% in 2011 and is estimated around mid-30s now. Cities: Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata (the three mega-cities of 2011), then Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad. A census town has 5,000 people, 75% non-farm male workers and density 400 per sq km. Problems: slums, traffic, floods, pollution, weak municipal finance.
Regional pattern of growth and density

The Gangetic plains, coasts and Kerala are densely settled; deserts, Himalaya and the Northeast are thin. Uttar Pradesh is the largest state by population; Sikkim is the smallest. Bihar has the highest density among states (1,106 per sq km in 2011); Arunachal Pradesh the lowest. Reasons: fertile alluvium, water, history of farming, and now job-centres. Low density in hill states reflects relief and climate.
Delimitation and population control

Seats in the Lok Sabha are frozen on 1971 numbers until the first census after 2026 (Articles 82 and 170). If seats follow today's population, northern states with higher growth gain and southern states lose share, though they did better at population control. The debate is about fairness: should success in family planning be penalised?
Schemes and planning

Smart Cities (2015), AMRUT (2015, urban water), Swachh Bharat (2014), PM Awas , and Mission Shakti for women. The National Population Policy 2000 set the goal of reaching replacement TFR; Mission Parivar Vikas targets high-fertility districts. Regional contrasts: Kerala sex ratio above 1,000; Haryana among the lowest.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the main features of India's demographic transition and the demographic dividend." (15 marks) "Examine the causes and consequences of rural-urban migration." (10 marks) Structure: data; theory; regional contrasts; opportunities and risks; schemes. Prelims tip: Census 2011 literacy is 74.04%, sex ratio 943; the replacement level TFR is 2.1.
Distribution of Key Natural Resources
Resources shape power

Oil built the Gulf's wealth and the world's wars. Cobalt and lithium will shape the next era. Where resources lie, who controls them, and how they are traded is a basic GS I theme, and it links to international relations.
Kinds of resources
Another split: biotic (forests, fish) and abiotic (minerals, water). Resources become reserves when they can be mined profitably. Technology and price change what counts as a resource.
Fossil fuels

Oil lies in a few basins: the Persian Gulf (about half of known reserves), the US, Russia and Canada's oil sands. Venezuela claims the largest proven reserves. OPEC (1960) has 12 members as of 2024 and OPEC+ includes Russia. Coal is widely spread and burned mostly for power and steel.
Metals

Iron ore lies in old shield areas, which is why Australia, Brazil, India and South Africa lead. Copper is concentrated along the Andes. Many figures change each year; check the latest USGS or industry data for exact ranks.
Critical minerals and the lithium triangle

Lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite and rare earths go into batteries, wind turbines and chips. The lithium triangle (Chile, Argentina, Bolivia) holds large brine reserves. The DR Congo supplies most cobalt, often with child labour. China processes most of the world's rare earths and battery materials, giving it leverage.
Water, forests and fisheries

Only about 2.5% of water is fresh, and most of that is in ice. Forests: Amazon , Congo basin , Siberian taiga, boreal Canada. Fisheries: Grand Banks, Peruvian anchovy, North Sea, East Asia. Overfishing is a global problem; the high seas have no single owner. UN High Seas treaty (BBNJ) was adopted in 2023.
Trade routes and chokepoints

Resources travel by sea through narrow straits: Hormuz (about a fifth of world oil), Malacca (between Indonesia and Malaysia, links the Indian and Pacific oceans), Bab-el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal . Attacks on shipping in the Red Sea since late 2023 pushed ships round the Cape of Good Hope. Pipelines such as Druzhba (Russia to Europe) matter for gas and oil on land.
Resource curse or blessing?

Many resource-rich states, such as Nigeria, Venezuela and DR Congo, suffer from corruption, conflict and a weak industry (the resource curse or "Dutch disease"). Others, like Norway, avoided it with a sovereign wealth fund and strong institutions. Resource nationalism (Indonesia banning raw nickel exports) is rising. The lesson: institutions decide outcomes.
India's resource position

India has coal, iron ore, bauxite and mica but imports about 85% of oil, most gas, and nearly all lithium and cobalt. It holds large thorium reserves. To fix this it uses strategic reserves , buys foreign assets via ONGC Videsh and KABIL, and joins the Minerals Security Partnership (2022). The Arctic and Antarctic (Himadri and Bharati stations) add a polar resource angle.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the global distribution of petroleum and its geopolitical implications." (15 marks) "Why are critical minerals central to the energy transition? What are India's vulnerabilities?" (15 marks) Structure: map the distribution; reasons (geology); trade patterns; politics; India's dependency and response. Prelims tip: Chile is the top copper miner; DR Congo has most cobalt; OPEC was founded in 1960 in Baghdad.
Factors in the Location of Industries Worldwide
Industry follows cost and opportunity

Why did steel go to the Ruhr and phones to Shenzhen? Why is the Rust Belt rusting? Location theory explains the map of world industry. In mains, answer with factors, a theory and a changing pattern , with Indian links.
Classic factors

Raw material (weight-losing industries stay near it), power (aluminium), market (bulky or perishable goods), labour (textiles), capital , transport , water , land , government policy (SEZs, tax breaks) and agglomeration , where firms cluster to share suppliers and workers. Industrial inertia means industries stay after the original reason has gone.
Weber and beyond

Weber (1909) gave the least-cost model. Hotelling (1929) added competition: sellers cluster to share the market. Losch looked at market areas. Vernon's product cycle (1966) suggested new products start in rich countries, then move to cheaper ones as they mature. Porter (1990) argued clusters create competitive advantage.
Major industrial regions

Traditional: Ruhr (Germany), Great Lakes (USA, steel and cars), Donbas (Ukraine), Midlands (UK), Kanto and Kansai (Japan). New: Pearl River Delta and Yangtze delta (China), Seoul, Taiwan, and Silicon Valley . Many older regions declined; some rebuilt themselves with services and technology.
Shifting centre of gravity
Reasons: cheaper labour, big markets, trade liberalisation, containerisation and global value chains. Brands design in one place and assemble in another.
Technology and footloose industries

Electronics, software and pharma depend on skills, research and airports more than on coal or ore. Their location depends on universities , venture capital and urban quality. 3D printing and AI may make production more local. Just-in-time supply (Toyota) shows how coordination matters as much as cost.
Case study: policy can create a location

China set up Special Economic Zones in 1980 (Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou, Xiamen) under Deng Xiaoping. A fishing town, Shenzhen became a global electronics hub within decades. Cheap labour was not enough: ports, tax breaks, foreign capital and WTO entry (2001) all helped. India's SEZ Act of 2005 copied the idea, with mixed results due to land and tax problems.
Reshoring, tariffs and supply chain risk

COVID-19 and trade wars exposed risks of concentrating in one country. The US CHIPS Act (2022), Europe's Chips Act and tariff moves aim to bring production home or to friendly states ("friend-shoring"). Critics fear higher prices and fragmentation. China remains central to most supply chains, so full decoupling is hard.
Where India fits

India aims to gain from China plus one . Apple's contract makers have set up in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka; autos cluster in Chennai, Pune and Gurugram; pharma in Hyderabad. India's PLI schemes and semiconductor mission (2021) seek fabs. Problems: logistics costs, land, power quality, and labour law. See also the lesson on Indian industrial regions.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the factors responsible for the shifting of the industrial centre of gravity to East Asia." (15 marks) "Why have older industrial regions of the world declined? Give examples." (10 marks) Structure: factors; theory; shift timeline; two examples; India's opportunity and obstacles. Prelims tip: Ruhr = coal and steel; Silicon Valley = software and chips; Pearl River Delta = electronics.
Population Theories and Settlements
Numbers, food and the places we live

Will the world run out of food? Why do cities have the shape they do? These two questions give us population theories and settlement geography. For mains, know who said what and when, and link to India's ageing, migration and cities.
Malthus, 1798

Thomas Malthus , An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798): population grows geometrically, food arithmetically. Positive checks (famine, disease, war) and preventive checks (late marriage, restraint) keep numbers in line. Neo-Malthusians (Paul Ehrlich, The Population Bomb , 1968; the Club of Rome's Limits to Growth , 1972) added resource limits.
Critics: Boserup and Marx

Ester Boserup , The Conditions of Agricultural Growth (1965), reversed the logic: population pressure forces innovation and intensive farming. "Necessity is the mother of invention." Marx said poverty arises from capitalist social structure, not from numbers. Green Revolution and technology so far have supported Boserup more than Malthus.
Transition and optimum population

Demographic transition (Thompson 1929, Notestein 1945) links fertility fall to development. Optimum population (Edwin Cannan; Alfred Sauvy) is the number that gives the best living standard with available resources. Above it is overpopulation, below it underpopulation. It is hard to measure because technology and trade shift the optimum.
Rural settlements

Pattern depends on terrain, water, defence and culture. In India, compact villages dominate the plains; dispersed hamlets in the hills, Northeast and tribal areas; linear villages along roads and rivers in Kerala and the Ganga valley.
Urban structure models

Burgess (1925) : concentric zones around the CBD (Chicago). Hoyt (1939) : wedges along transport lines. Harris and Ullman (1945) : several nuclei. Indian cities show mixtures with colonial cores and slum pockets.
Central place theory

Walter Christaller (1933) said settlements form a hierarchy: many villages, fewer towns, one city. Each serves a market area. Higher-order goods need a larger threshold and range. Hexagons are the most efficient shape.
City size and hierarchy

Primate city (Mark Jefferson, 1939): a city far bigger than the next, such as Bangkok or Paris. Rank-size rule (Zipf): the nth city is 1/n of the biggest. Conurbation (Patrick Geddes, 1915): merged towns, like Greater Manchester. Megacity : above 10 million people.
Is overpopulation the problem?

Neo-Malthusians point to climate and water limits. Others say consumption , not numbers, drives the pressure, since the richest countries use far more resources per head. Many countries now face falling fertility and ageing (Japan, China, South Korea). A balanced view: both numbers and consumption matter, and outcomes depend on policy.
India: settlements and slums

Indian cities are marked by primate-like growth (Mumbai, Delhi) and by slums; Dharavi in Mumbai is a well-known case. Smart Cities and AMRUT target infrastructure, and the Census defines towns. Many Indian villages are clustered along caste lines; rural-urban fringes see "peri-urban" sprawl.
How to write this

Likely questions "Critically examine Malthusian theory in the Indian context." (10 marks) "Discuss the urban land-use models and their relevance to Indian cities." (15 marks) Structure: theory, year, author; strengths; criticism; Indian evidence (Green Revolution, ageing, migration). Prelims tip: Malthus 1798; Boserup 1965; Burgess 1925 concentric; Christaller 1933 central place.
Salient Features of World Physical Geography
A mental map saves marks

Prelims and mains both reward a clear mental map of the world: where mountains, rivers, seas and straits lie. This lesson is a revision capsule. Learn it with an atlas open and quiz yourself on locations.
Continents and oceans
Mountain systems
Most great ranges follow plate boundaries. The Pacific "Ring of Fire" circles the Pacific with young fold mountains and volcanoes (Andes, Rockies, Japan).
Rivers

The Nile and the Amazon are often argued as the longest; recent studies suggest the Amazon could be as long as or longer. For exams, the safe answer is the Nile . Rivers draining to enclosed seas include the Volga (Caspian) and the Amu and Syr Darya (Aral).
Lakes and deserts

The Great Lakes of North America hold a large share of surface fresh water; Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake by area. Lake Baikal is the deepest and holds about 20% of the world's liquid fresh water. Deserts: Sahara, Arabian, Gobi, Atacama (driest), Kalahari, Thar. Antarctica is the largest by area.
Straits, canals and chokepoints

Suez Canal (opened 1869) links the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. Panama Canal (1914) links the Atlantic and Pacific. Straits: Gibraltar, Bosphorus, Hormuz, Malacca, Bab-el-Mandeb, Bering. These control the flow of oil, grain and goods, and are central to international relations.
Lines on the globe

Latitude lines are parallel; longitudes meet at the poles. The Prime Meridian runs through Greenwich; the International Date Line follows 180 degrees. The Sun is overhead between the Tropics. Days become polar near the circles.
Facts that change

Everest was officially re-measured at 8,848.86 m by China and Nepal in 2020. The Aral Sea has shrunk drastically since 1960 because of cotton irrigation. Arctic sea ice and glaciers are in retreat. Treat many "record" numbers as approximate and say "about" or "as of" in answers.
India's place on the world map

The mainland lies between 8 and 37 degrees N, so the Tropic of Cancer splits it nearly in half. India is the seventh largest country by area and has land borders with six countries (seven if Afghanistan is counted through PoK). Himalaya and the Indian Ocean frame it. The Indian Ocean linking Africa, the Gulf and East Asia explains India's sea power role.
How to write this

Likely questions "Mention the major straits and canals of the world and explain their strategic importance." (10 marks) "Locate on a map and explain the importance of the Malacca Strait." (10 marks) Structure: locate; give a number; add one strategic or economic point; link to India. Prelims tip: sketch a rough world map and drill locations of seas, straits, deserts and mountain ranges.
Changes in Critical Geographical Features
Maps are being redrawn

Glaciers retreat, lakes dry up, coasts move and species shift. GS I asks you to explain causes and effects of such changes, from sea-level rise to the death of the Aral Sea. Always separate natural cycles from human-driven change.
What has changed

Global average temperature is about 1.1 to 1.2 C above the 1850-1900 level (IPCC AR6, 2021). 2024 was the warmest year on record and the first calendar year above 1.5 C (WMO, as of 2025). Greenhouse gases from fossil fuels, cement and land-use change are the main cause. Ice, oceans and living things all respond.
Ice caps and glaciers
Arctic summer sea ice is shrinking by about 12% a decade. Greenland and Antarctica lose ice, and the Thwaites glacier is a worry. Melting sea ice does not raise sea level directly; land ice does.
Sea level rise

Sea level has risen about 20 cm since 1900 and the rate is now about 4 mm a year (IPCC AR6, WMO). The coasts of deltas, small islands and big port cities (Mumbai, Kolkata, Dhaka, Jakarta) are most at risk.
Water bodies: lakes and seas
Causes are mostly human: diversion for irrigation, groundwater pumping and urban growth, plus drought. Effects: dust storms, loss of fisheries, health hazards and migration.
Flora and fauna

Species move to cooler places, up hills and towards the poles. Coral reefs bleach when seas get hotter; the world is in a fourth global bleaching event (2023 onward, NOAA). Forests face fires and pests. Habitat loss, over-exploitation, invasive species and pollution add pressure: the IPBES report of 2019 warned that about a million species face extinction.
Permafrost, glaciers and hazards

Thawing permafrost releases methane and CO2 and damages roads and pipelines in Siberia and Alaska. Mountain glaciers feed glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) . Himalayan glaciers are retreating on average, and the 2023 South Lhonak lake burst in Sikkim damaged the Teesta III dam.
Tipping points: are we past them?

Scientists warn of tipping points : collapse of the West Antarctic ice sheet, Amazon dieback, Atlantic circulation slowdown, coral die-off. Timing is uncertain, but the risk rises with each tenth of a degree. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims at under 2 C. Critics doubt the pledges are enough; developing countries ask for climate finance and equity.
India's exposed features

Sundarbans are losing land (Ghoramara island has lost much area). The Himalayan glaciers (Gangotri retreat), the Western Ghats' shifting rainfall, and coastal Gujarat and Odisha face salt intrusion. Marine heatwaves threaten the Gulf of Mannar. India's National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008) has eight missions, and its net-zero target is 2070.
How to write this

Likely questions "How are melting glaciers and rising seas changing the geography of coasts? Illustrate with Indian examples." (15 marks) "Discuss the causes and consequences of the shrinking of the Aral Sea." (10 marks) Structure: cause (human and natural); evidence (data); effect on land, water, life and people; adaptation and mitigation. Prelims tip: ice-albedo feedback; melting sea ice does not raise sea level; GLOF; Ramsar sites are wetlands.
Disaster Types and India's Vulnerability
Nature gives hazards; people make disasters

India sits on active plates, borders a warming ocean and has a monsoon climate. Millions of poor and unprepared people live in exposed places. UPSC treats disasters as geography (causes) and as governance (response). This lesson covers the first part.
Hazard, risk and vulnerability

A hazard is a dangerous event. A disaster happens when a hazard hits a vulnerable community. The Disaster Management Act, 2005 defines a disaster as a catastrophe, mishap, calamity or grave occurrence that causes loss of life, property or damage to the environment beyond the community's capacity to cope.
Classification

Another split is by speed: rapid onset (earthquake, flash flood) and slow onset (drought, desertification). Disasters can cascade: a quake triggers a landslide, which blocks a river and floods a valley.
India's vulnerability: the numbers
These figures come from NDMA and similar sources; they change with updated maps. Most districts face at least one major hazard. Heat waves and lightning are now recognised as major killers.
Why India is so exposed

Geography : young Himalaya, a long coast, river basins in flood plains. Climate : monsoon variability, and warming seas. Society : dense population, poor housing, weak enforcement of building codes, encroachment on floodplains, and deforestation. Poverty is the biggest vulnerability, as poor people live in kutcha houses on risky land.
Major disasters to remember

Bhopal gas leak (1984), Odisha super cyclone (1999), Bhuj quake (2001), Indian Ocean tsunami (2004), Mumbai floods (2005), Uttarakhand floods (2013), Chennai floods (2015), Kerala floods (2018), Chamoli (2021), Wayanad landslides (July 2024, over 200 deaths), Himachal and Sikkim floods (2023).
Why each hazard strikes

Floods : heavy monsoon rain, silt-choked rivers (Kosi, the "sorrow of Bihar"), poor drainage, encroachment. Cyclones : warm Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea, shallow coastal shelf. Drought : monsoon failure, rain-shadow areas (Marathwada, Rayalaseema, Bundelkhand). Landslides : steep young slopes, heavy rain, road cutting and tunnelling. Heat waves : dry north-west winds and clear skies in April-June. Cloudbursts : rain above 10 cm in an hour over a small area in the hills.
Are disasters really "natural"?

Scholars argue that disasters are social : the same quake kills thousands in a poor country and few in a rich one. Kerala 2018 and Chennai 2015 followed unplanned building on wetlands and bad dam management. Others stress that climate change is increasing the hazards themselves. Both views matter: reduce exposure and vulnerability, and cut emissions.
Changing risk profile

Cities are the new frontier: urban floods in Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Delhi. Heat waves (2024 saw record temperatures in north India) and lightning kill many each year. Himalayan states face glacial floods and landslides. India has the Vulnerability Atlas (BMTPC) for housing and a national flood and landslide mapping effort.
How to write this

Likely questions "Discuss the vulnerability profile of India to natural hazards." (15 marks) "Why are urban floods increasing in India? Suggest measures." (10 marks) Structure: define; classify; numbers; causes (natural plus human); recent cases; link to the framework in the next lesson. Prelims tip: DM Act 2005; Sendai Framework (2015-2030); Bhopal 1984 is the worst industrial disaster; Kerala floods 2018.
Disaster Management Framework in India
Moving from relief to resilience

Until 1999 India saw disasters as the job of the relief commissioner and Agriculture Ministry. The Odisha super cyclone (1999) and Bhuj quake (2001) changed that. Today law, funds and forces exist; the debate is about preparedness, federalism and local capacity.
The disaster management cycle
Mitigation (structural: embankments, codes; non-structural: zoning, laws), preparedness (warning, drills), response (search and rescue, relief), and recovery (rehabilitation, "build back better").
How the system evolved

1999 : High Powered Committee under J.C. Pant. 2001 : Gujarat quake, a national committee, and 10th Finance Commission. 2005 : the Disaster Management Act . 2006 : the NDRF. 2009 : National Policy on Disaster Management. 2016 : first National Disaster Management Plan, updated 2019 , aligned with the Sendai Framework.
Institutions under the 2005 Act
The National Executive Committee (headed by the Home Secretary) assists NDMA. The National Institute of Disaster Management (NIDM) trains. The Ministry of Home Affairs is the nodal ministry.
Money and forces

Allocation follows the Finance Commission . The 15th FC (2021-26) set a framework for mitigation and capacity-building funds. States also have SDRF forces. Warning agencies: IMD (cyclone, rain), CWC (flood), INCOIS (tsunami), GSI (landslide).
The Sendai Framework, 2015-2030

Adopted in Sendai, Japan. It has four priorities : understanding risk, strengthening governance, investing in resilience, and better preparedness plus "build back better". It sets seven global targets: cut deaths, affected people, losses and raise early-warning cover. India launched the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) in 2019.
Hazard-wise mitigation

Earthquake : seismic building codes (IS 1893), retrofitting, land-use zoning. Flood : embankments, reservoirs, floodplain zoning, forecasts and ending encroachment. Cyclone : shelters, mangroves and shelter belts, early warning and evacuation. Drought : watershed work, crop planning, insurance. Landslide : slope stabilisation, hazard maps, regulating roads. Heat wave : Heat Action Plans, as in Ahmedabad (2013), now in many cities. Structural measures need money and time; non-structural ones (laws, awareness, drills) are cheaper and often more effective.
Centralised or local? "National disaster"?

The Act has no category called "national disaster"; it speaks of disasters of severe nature (L3). Kerala (2018) and Wayanad (2024) raised demands for a formal tag and more central money. Critics also say NDMA is weak in implementation and states under-use mitigation funds. Experts call for stronger local bodies and urban disaster authorities. The Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 moved in this direction.
